In a recent development, hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

It has been revealed that I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Recent findings suggest that absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

Sources indicate that one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

According to recent reports, there is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

According to recent reports, another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Sources indicate that thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something newly introduced to admire.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.
  • My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

Recent findings suggest that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

Sources indicate that in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

In a recent development, sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy states she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what newly introduced plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. This is senior editor Patrick McCombe. In this episode, Ian and Randy help Patrick address listener feedback and answer their questions. Guy is wondering if minisplits are a good idea. Matt asks how to build a bathroom that stands up to humidity. Keith asks for feedback on his made-for-quiet roof assembly. Patrick asks if roof coatings made to extend the life of shingle roofs are snake oil.

Please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

Ian: Painting in cooler temperatures, hiding ductwork.

Randy: Duct airtightness testing.

Patrick: Plenum trusses for hiding HVAC ductwork with Jake Bruton.

It was great meeting Randy at the most recent International Builders’ Show in Florida!

I am glad to hear Ian is happy with his Mr. Cool. I think they make a good product and have one myself. I am the dubious owner of six minisplit systems across four houses. I was all for them at first, but after multiple early failures my excitement began to fade. The problem is poor air filtration and mold growth. Because they don’t filter the air well, they become full of dust and mold.

I have a minisplit head-unit cleaning kit that gets a lot of use. After just one year of use, the minisplit fans become packed full of dust and the mold that comes with it. If you blueprint on getting a minisplit, plan for at least an annual cleaning. You’ll need about an hour to do a good job, and you will be horrified by the color of the water flowing out of the cleaning process—it’ll look a lot like what you’d find in a carpet cleaner’s dirty-water tank.

The houses I own are Airbnbs that are cleaned at least weekly and are in good condition. For a guy who works in indoor air quality consulting, I’ve been very disappointed with minisplits. From now on, I’m sticking with ducted systems that have real return-air ducts and filtration.

Thanks for the great show as always.

In a recent development, from Patrick: Hi Guy, Good to hear from you, as always. Thanks for sharing your thoughts on minisplits. On the subject, I read “The Hidden Costs of Minisplits” yesterday by Allison Bailes. Pretty horrifying!

In a recent development, longtime reader, first-time poster here. Thank you all for generously sharing your knowledge and experience. I’ve learned a great deal.

My dilemma is the remodel of my main bathroom. My three kids like to pretend it’s a sauna and take 25-minute showers in succession until the giant mirror has water running down it and it looks like its raining. Not so cool for mold growth and material longevity.

It has been revealed that my question is: Can I put plywood—or something similar—on the ceiling behind the drywall when redo the room? Could this lead to more complications? Is my thought process backwards? I would like to prevent any nail pops, torn seams, or movement.

The house was built in 1984 and is a two-story Colonial with a truss roof framed at 24 inches on center. The attic is baffled and insulated with R-60 blown-in insulation. I have about 21 in. of insulation above, and I’d like to make future remodeling easier and less disruptive by avoiding the need to remove or disturb all that insulation just to replace the ceiling.

Sources indicate that FHB has recently been hearing about roof coatings that claim to renew aging asphalt shingles and give them an additional 10 years of life. I was immediately skeptical. The first time we heard from someone it was a question on Instagram about their mom’s little house in Florida.

To me, it sounds like the coatings that are used on RVs. Have you heard of these products? This product, marketed to an elderly homeowner, reminded me of the aluminum siding boom of the 1950s and ’60s. Do you think elastomeric roof coatings ever have a legitimate place in residential roofing?

In a recent development, welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. Ian: I hope you’re done painting. It’s been getting cold at night around here.

Randy: Is your furnace and ductwork all done?

Patrick: Tool test of cordless oscillating multitools by Aaron Miiller.

Off-site construction is a subject that needs more attention in the US. I’m glad that Tedd Benson keeps getting good press.

Kevin sent us a Boston Globe editorial piece describing why Massachusetts needs more modular or manufactured housing. It mentions Bensonwood and quotes Mark Hetzlera, a Bensonwood employee. It’s an editorial, not a reported piece, so it shouldn’t be held to the same standards as journalism. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board.

Make it Easier to Build More Modular Housing.

I’m an owner-builder in Bay City, Oregon, in Marine Climate Zone 4C. I’m planning a single-slope roof with a 3:12 pitch and a 24-ft. clear span using parallel-chord trusses. My assembly plan consists of standing-seam aluminum roofing over purlins, 4 in. of continuous polyiso, taped Zip sheathing as the primary air barrier, and a truss cavity filled with 8 in. of mineral wool or fiberglass batts, for a target total insulation value of R-56. The interior will be acoustic fabric (a black muslin theater fabric) and then wood slats with gaps to form an acoustic ceiling. I’m not planning for an interior membrane planned so the acoustic function works as designed.

My question is: With 4 in. of exterior polyiso and Zip sheathing serving as the primary air barrier, what building science function would an additional interior air or vapor-control layer serve? Would an acoustically open ceiling be compatible with this assembly, or am I missing a key risk? If so, do you have any ideas how I might make this work?

Recent findings suggest that thanks for all you do. I appreciate any guidance and absolutely LOVE the show!

One last thing: As a former radio host, I appreciate good voices, and Ian’s is so distinctive and awesome! It reminds me of Patrick Warburton, the actor who voices Officer Joe Swanson on Family Guy.

Sources indicate that as a fellow Oregonian, I know the 4C climate zone well. In a lot of ways, its a Goldilocks zone—not too humid, not too dry. The climate tends to be pretty forgiving, with the exception of our frequent rains.

According to recent reports, as I evaluate assemblies, I always define and break out the control layers to see if there are any issues. Beyond water, air, vapor, and thermal, it is good to consider wind and fire control layers. The most glaring omission I see is a well-defined water control layer. I consider roofing to be a water-shedding layer, as water can get through via penetrations, mistakes, etc. You proposal to use polyiso, but you didn’t specify the facer type. In our area, the most commonly used facer in the roofing community is fiberglass faced, but aluminum facer is easily sourced, too. The former would make a terrible water control layer and the latter would be okay, except you would have to tape all the seams, and aluminum isn’t the most durable. I would start by installing a self-adhered WRB or roof underlayment directly on top of the polyiso. The permeability doesn’t really matter (more on that to come). This would be your primary bulk-water control layer. The next most important layer is the air control layer. As long as you tape the seams of the Zip sheathing, you should be good there. Pay attention to how  the roof air barrier connects to the wall air barrier to maintain continuity.

According to recent reports, for vapor control, of all the materials in this assembly, foil-faced polyiso would be the least permeable, as it is a Class 1 vapor barrier. If the polyiso is fiberglass-faced, it is a Class 3 semi-permeable vapor retarder, with a permeance of roughly 1 to 4 perms. The OSB in the Zip is roughly the same at 3 perms. In one sense, vapor control becomes less of a concern because you have created a vented assembly with the purlins below the metal roofing. In another sense, it may be a moot point because the thickness of the insulation should keep the Zip sheathing warm enough to prevent condensation. At approximately R-20, the exterior insulation would also meet the code requirement in our area. If vapor were to pass through, it would simply get whisked away via the vented gap. If you were to put a vapor-closed roof underlayment on top of the fiberglass-faced polyiso, the combination would essentially a layer similar to foil facing. In both cases, you are fine because the insulation is thick enough to keep condensation from forming on the bottom side of the Zip. If anything, a vapor-open membrane would be slightly more resilient, but we are splitting hairs in the weeds at this point.

Industry observers note that for the thermal control layer, the main change I would make is to switch to two layers of 2-in. polyiso boards in lieu of one 4-in. layer. Rigid insulation is prone to shrink, and by offsetting the seams you will avoid numerous thermal breaks throughout the assembly. On the interior, pick whichever fluffy insulation you like. Eight inches should work well, but adding a few more Rs wouldn’t hurt, either. From a wind-washing control perspective, mineral wool and wood fiber are denser than fiberglass, so I would consider those. One wants to avoid the thermal degradation from wind washing– think about a sweater on a windy day.

Sources indicate that patrick’s point about the fire control is valid. If you were to install a layer of Sheetrock and fire-tape it, its vapor-open nature means it wouldn’t affect the assembly at all. From a sound-control perspective, you might consider applying an elastomeric acoustic sealant and/or installing resilient channels before hanging the Sheetrock. From that point, adding the black muslin fabric and wood slats would work well.

Recent findings suggest that I’m reaching out for some guidance. Earlier this summer during a storm, we lost a large tree in front of our house. It turns out that a good afternoon shade tree can cover up a few building science sins. In the 19 years we’ve lived here, we’ve gotten by with our AC air handler in the unconditioned attic. But without that tree blocking much of the afternoon and setting sun, the AC has clearly been working harder this summer, making it obvious that more than a newly introduced tree is needed.

I realize step one is getting a proper energy audit, but in the meantime I have a few questions:.

Sorry for the length of the letter, but I feel like this has all snowballed on me and could really use your help getting this project organized.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).

Sources indicate that the district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes. It relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the tariff case I helped litigate. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds.

In a recent development, we are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono. Stanford Law School Prof. and former federal judge Michael McConnell, also worked with us on the brief. He is one of the nation's leading experts on executive power, a prominent conservative originalist constitutional law scholar, and was our lead counsel in the Supreme Court phase of the IEEPA tariff case.

Here is a summary of our arguments:.

As the Supreme Court emphasized in its recent decisions striking down Donald Trump's Massive IEEPA tariffs, "the Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people." Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 241 (2026)  The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, "the most vital of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union." Just months ago, the Supreme Court in Learning Resources applied those fundamental principles to hold that the President may not use a general grant of authority to "regulate … importation" to impose tariffs, because the power to "regulate" is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power. This case asks whether the same President—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a "restriction" on entry—may accomplish by a different label what Learning Resources forbade.

The exaction here is a tax. Its "defining feature" is that it raises revenue. Learning Resources, 607 U.S. at 241. It is neither a mere fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. The power to "restrict" entry is not the power to "tax" entry. To limit or qualify entry notes nothing about charging for it, and the Government can identify no statute in which the words "restrict" or "restriction" confer tax authority.

Sources indicate that the Immigration and Nationality Act  contains express, detailed provisions for fees and payments, setting each amount and specifying how the funds are collected and spent. This confirms the absence of a generalized, unlimited discretionary presidential taxing power. Congress does not "hide elephants in mouseholes," and this case involves a very large elephant. Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass'ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001). In more than a century, no President has used Section 212(f) or Section 215(a) of the INA to raise revenue, a point the Government does not dispute. As the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, that absence is "strong evidence" the power does not exist.

In a recent development, in addition, the government's interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political issue to the executive. The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive.

I have previously criticized the $100,000 H-1B fee on both legal and policy grounds here, here, and here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp. v. Trump, the first case challenging Donald Trump's massive 50% Section 338 tariffs against Canadian imports. The plaintiff is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That case resulted in the tariffs' invalidation by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch, and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.

We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice. Here is a summary of our key arguments, which should soon be posted at the Cato website:.

This brief explains why Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 cannot be used to impose the tariffs enacted by Defendants, and why doing so violates the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

Sources indicate that the Court should strike down the Section 338 duties for three reasons. First, Section 338 requires that any tariffs imposed be in response to discriminatory trade restrictions enacted by foreign trading partners, and that those tariffs "offset" the barriers imposed by those countries. The Section 338 tariffs imposed by the Trump administration violate both of these requirements. In addition, Section 338 has been superseded by later statutes and is no longer operative.

It has been revealed that second, the major questions doctrine forecloses interpreting Section 338 to permit the President to impose extraordinary import taxes whenever another country imposes any trade restrictions or declines to purchase American goods. to "speak clearly" when it assigns to the executive "decisions of vast 'economic and political significance.'" The sweeping power claimed by the administration in this case undeniably raises a major question, and it is at the very least unclear that Section 338 actually grants such vast authority.

Third, stripping the statute's qualitative conditions of operative force violates the nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegation of legislative power to the executive. An extremely high rate ceiling of 50 percent cannot substitute for clear legislative limiting how and when tariffs can be imposed.

Cato and I (together with Prof. Michael McConnell) also recently submitted an amicus brief in litigation challenging Trump's massive Section 301 tariffs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v. RAICES, a case challenging the legality of Donald Trump's January 2025 "invasion" executive order, which bars virtually all legal migration across the southern border. Trump relies on the Guarantee Clause of Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution, which states that "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government, and shall protect each of them against Invasion." The administration claims that illegal migration, drug smuggling, and supposed "public health" risks  qualify as an "invasion" under the Guarantee Clause, thereby authorizing the president to suspend legal migration indefinitely.

The Trump administration's position on this issue is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications. In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion" I provide a comprehensive overview of the many reasons why "invasion" - as that term is used in the Constitution and the AEA - must be a military attack, not illegal migration, drug smuggling, or other similar activity. As James Madison put it, "invasion is an operation of war." I provided a shorter overview of the invasion order and its dangerous implications in a 2025 Just Security article.

Industry observers note that I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion. Among other things, it would allow the federal government to suspend the writ of habeas corpus (and thereby detain people - including US citizens - without due process) at any time. It would also give state governments the power to "engage in war" against neighboring foreign countries at virtually any time, even without congressional authorization. And there is much more. This case has major implications that go beyond immigration, and threaten the civil liberties of US citizens, as well as recent migrants.

It has been revealed that the Supreme Court could potentially rule against Trump on statutory grounds, without reaching the issue of the definition of "invasion" in the Constitution. That is what the district court and the DC Circuit did. Alternatively, the Court could rule that the president has purely statutory authority to bar these migrants. But if it rejects these statutory arguments, or at least does so in large part, it will have to reach the "invasion" issue. If the justices do reach that issue, it is vital that the reject the administration's position.

There are also a number of procedural issues in the case (primarily involving the scope of the remedy), which I will not attempt to go over here.

Recent findings suggest that this case should not be confused with the related ongoing litigation over the legality of Trump's invocation of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. The AEA can only be used to detain and deport migrants when there is a declared war, an "invasion," or a "predatory incursion." There, too, the Trump administration claims illegal migration and drug smuggling qualify as an "invasion," and there too it is wrong to do so (on which see  Part III of my article, my amicus brief in the Fifth Circuit AEA case, which I coauthored on behalf of the Brennan Center, the Cato Institute, and others). As detailed in my article, it is highly likely that "invasion" has the same meaning in the AEA and in the four places where that term is used in the Constitution, enacted just a few years earlier.

According to recent reports, I will likely have more to say about this case in future posts and other writings. Stay tuned!

Border Search of Immigration Lawyer's Phone Was Likely Unconstitutional Retaliation for Lawyer's Speech

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S.
  • Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025.
  • It has been revealed that in late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Judge Allison Burroughs (D. Mass.) Friday in Lattarulo v. Mullin:.

Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters," which regularly "amasses hundreds of thousands of views." Georges Cote is currently being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations ("HSI"), the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), for employing individuals without a legal right to work in the United States.

Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025. Unlike Lattarulo, "Cote is not an immigration attorney—he focuses on personal injury." The firm responded on September 12, 2025, and the government sent Cote a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, 2025. The firm was given ten days to attempt to verify the identity and work authorization of the employees named in the Notice of Suspect Documents.

It has been revealed that in late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip. On September 27, 2025, Cote arrived back at Logan Airport from Aruba without glitch. Lattarulo made the same journey the following day, September 28, 2025. Lattarulo passed through customs preclearance in Aruba before boarding a flight to Boston.

When his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP") agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

The seized cell phone data is presently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits. The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo's clients. {The Government was clear that any search of the contents of the phone would utilize a taint team to protect privileged information.} ….

The court held that Lattarulo was likely correct on his claim that the search was unconstitutional retaliation for his speech, and therefore granted "a preliminary injunction enjoining Defendants from accessing the data obtained from the phone before this action is resolved":.

"[T]he law is settled that as a general matter the First Amendment prohibits government officials from subjecting an individual to retaliatory actions, including criminal prosecutions, for speaking out." … The retaliation problem [here] turns on causation—that is, whether the seizure and search of Lattarulo's cell phone would have occurred but for his protected speech.

Respondents have provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise. Indeed, Lattarulo's evidence suggests that any pursuit of criminal charges against employers for employing unauthorized immigrants is exceedingly rare. The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual.

The stage of the investigation at which the search occurred further bolsters the inference of pretext. Under HSI's own policies, the agency "presumes that employers who, within 10 business days of receiving a Notice of Suspect Documents, verify the identity and/or employment authorization of the listed employees, or take appropriate actions to address the apparent employment of unauthorized workers, have demonstrated reasonable care under the INA." The government's search occurred only three days after Georges Cote first received a Notice of Suspect Documents, meaning that the agency was still early in its period of "presum[ing]" compliance when it occurred. Thus, the government's actions here required it to short-circuit its orderly investigative procedures and cast aside its ten-day presumption of compliance in favor of immediately seizing Lattarulo's phone. That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive.

It has been revealed that further, Lattarulo has identified an "otherwise similarly situated individual not engaged in the same sort of protected speech," who was not subjected to the same enforcement action: his law firm partner Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights. Indeed, if the government was truly intent on seizing evidence at the first possible opportunity, Mr. Cote, who returned to America a full day before Lattarulo, would have been a more logical target. Nonetheless, the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search. The balance of the evidence at the moment before the Court thus suggests that Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech.

{It is true that the presence of probable cause generally precludes a finding of causation in a retaliatory arrest case, but the Supreme Court has recognized a limited exception for situations in which officers who "have probable cause to make arrests [for a particular crime] … typically exercise their discretion not to do so," such as "an individual who has been vocally complaining about police conduct … [before being] arrested for jaywalking," By analogy, the limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at concern here and that Lattarulo's own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property.}.

Recent findings suggest that it is true that Defendants can "prevail … by showing that the [search] would have been initiated without respect to retaliation," and here Defendants state that they have additional evidence which would show as much, but they have not provided it because they assert that doing so would prejudice an ongoing investigation…. [T]he Court concludes that the limited record that is before the Court suggests that Lattarulo is likely to succeed on the merits of his First Amendment retaliation claim and that the record before it is therefore adequate to grant the limited preliminary relief contemplated by this order.

The court didn't resolve Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim, because it granted the preliminary injunction based on the First Amendment claim. But it did note the following:.

Plaintiffs' Fourth Amendment claim turns largely on the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement. That exception "is grounded in the government's 'inherent authority to protect, and a paramount interest in protecting, its territorial integrity.'" It allows the government to perform "routine" border searches of electronic devices without suspicion of any crime, and to perform "non-routine" border searches of electronic devices without a warrant, so long as the government has reasonable suspicion. Alasaad v. Mayorkas (1st Cir. 2021).

Industry observers note that the question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband" or for "evidence of contraband or a border-related crime." Later in its opinion, however, it stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband, evidence of contraband, or for evidence of activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE." In most cases, of course, "border-related crime[s]" and "activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" are synonymous, and the First Circuit in Alasaad appears to have intended to use those terms more or less synonymously.

It has been revealed that the difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at issue—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is "enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" but arguably is not a "border-related crime." Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo's border crossing (or, more broadly, the government's interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government's border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.

Even though the suspected violation involves aliens and a law administered by ICE, the Court is not convinced that the First Circuit in Alasaad intended for the border exception to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception. Nonetheless, given the novelty of these questions and the fact that a ruling on them is not necessary, the Court will refrain at this point from reaching a firm conclusion on the concern of the border search's applicability….

Recent findings suggest that mary Lemay and Patrick M. Hanley (Butters Brazilian LLP) represent Lattarulo.

Latest Update: National Security Division Introduces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
  • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
  • Recent findings suggest that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The tech giant agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

Recent findings suggest that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

According to recent reports, “HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Industry observers note that pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Recent findings suggest that although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

According to recent reports, this case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

Industry observers note that welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. This is senior editor Patrick McCombe. I’m joined by Green Building Advisor editor Randy Williams, Fine Homebuilding contributing editor and operations manager for TDS Design/Build in Madison, Wisconsin, and producer Cari Delahanty.

Please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

Ian: House painting, interesting TDS projects.

Randy: Green Building Advisor updates.

Patrick: Upcoming article about surge protection by Chad McClung.

Grant referred to a house where he recently stayed as a “tiny house,” describing it as being about 16 ft. x 30 ft. I guess I have lived in a “tiny house” for 20 years! Ours is a Cape, built in 1953 by the people from whom we bought it. It has a 24-ft. x 26-ft. footprint and no dormer.

Recent findings suggest that as discussed on the podcast, there are a lot of great things about a house this size. However, it is, in fact, too small. It is too small to comfortably fit furniture or closets or a family to gather to watch a movie. Our “primary bedroom” is 10 ft. x 11 ft. with a small closet out of that boundary.

The full house could be arranged to be a very nice size for a couple, but it feels too small for four of us, especially with only one bathroom. I’m not sure how we’ve worked out the lack of closet space and single bathroom with three women plus me, but we have. When my daughters were in high school, I found it emotionally uncomfortable that most of their friends had bigger and nicer homes.

Putting my hurt ego aside, I feel they are lucky to be able to appreciate future living spaces that will likely be more luxurious than they are used to. My oldest daughter definitely had a better bedroom at college and easier access to a bathroom!

Discussion of Chris Briley’s recent low-voltage lighting article on Green Building Advisor.

This article, “Low Voltage Lighting,” is from Chris’ Pretty Good House blog. Chris suggests that given the low energy consumption of LED lighting, do we still need line voltage lighting circuits anymore? Randy, can you briefly explain Chris’s premise? What do you think as an electrician? Does it make sense to switch our wiring methods for modern lighting? Ian, what do you think about this?

When you look at a finished house, what are the small details that make you feel the builder really took the time to do things right?

I’m not talking about expensive finishes or high-end appliances. I’m thinking more about the little things that might not stand out in photos but make a difference once you actually live in the house—clean trim work, well-planned storage, good lighting, quiet doors, sensible outlets, properly finished transitions, etc.

According to recent reports, I’ve noticed that some of the most enjoyable spaces aren’t necessarily the most expensive ones. They just seem to have fewer little annoyances because someone thought through how the space would actually be used.

For those of you who have built or remodeled homes, what is one relatively small detail you’re especially glad you included? And is there anything you wish you’d thought about before construction was finished?

I’m curious whether the things people appreciate most are usually visible design choices or the less noticeable details behind the walls and throughout the house.

We talked about what gives you confidence in a builder, so now let’s talk about what you see most often on construction sites that is done poorly or incorrectly?

Thanks to Randy, Ian, and Cari for joining me and thanks to all of you for listening. Remember to send us your questions and suggestions to [email protected] and please like, comment, or review us no matter how you’re listening–it helps other folks find our podcast.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs.
  • Industry observers note that I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is a wrap. I have attended every NLC since I was a 1L in 2006 (except for the cancelled COVID year). At each convention, the focus is a bit different but the overall takeaway is similar. There is a healthy a mix of timeless topics and topical topics, with an infusion of the political landscape of the day. It is very hard to capture the essence of a convention by watching some or even all of the panels, as so much business transpires in the hallways and at the bars.

Recent findings suggest that I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs. For example, CNN blared "After blue wave, Federalist Society is ready to move on from Trump." Really? Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered the Olson Lecture, White House Counsel Will Scharf had a fireside chat, White House Advisor May Mailman discussed over-regulation, and Gene Hamilton favored restrictive immigration policy on behalf of America First Legal Foundation. Plus there were other members of the administration from the EPA and OLP.

Industry observers note that I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation. I don't think anyone actually knows exactly what to do. The midterm election, of course, was the elephant in the room. I offered my take here. A lot can happen over the next two years.

It has been revealed that I'm flummoxed by the uproar about the commemorative coins celebrating Calais, Slaughter, and other decision. These were in fact generational wins at the Supreme Court. Justice Scalia established overruling Humphrey's Executor as a founding principle of FedSoc. Since the 1980s, conservatives--including John Roberts--have seen the Voting Rights Act as violating the Constitution. And West Virginia v. B.P.J. was such an obvious outcome--except perhaps at CNN. Plus, this was the swaggiest NLC I've ever been to. There was an entire room to pick up FedSoc swag. The coins were a nice touch.

In a recent development, perhaps the biggest disruption at the convention was the groundstop. My flight home Saturday evening was cancelled, as were many others. I was able to get a room at the Mayflower for another day. Fortunately, one of the few remaining perks of United status is priority rebooking during "irregular operations." I was originally scheduled to fly home Sunday evening around 7:30 p.m. The United App has a new feature that lets you be on standby for up to three flights at once without losing your confirmed seat. United will send you a text notifying you that a seat opened up on an earlier flight, and you have twenty minutes to accept it. I was able to jump from the 7:30 p.m. flight to the 12:50 p.m. flight. A few hours later, I was given a chance to jump from the 12:50 p.m. flight to the 10:58 a.m. flight. For both of these flights, I was number one on the standby list. Around 5:00 a.m., I was offered the chance to move to the 8:20 a.m. flight, but I was sleeping and missed the window. The system worked very well. And without my status, I doubt I would have been able to get the earlier flight. As things turned out, the 12:50 p.m. flight was cancelled. I will get home today.

How to Get Stink Bugs Out of Your House

📅 18 Nov 2015 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, the brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is a stowaway from Asia that entered the U.S.
  • As of 2021, the brown marmorated stink bug had been found in 47 states, and it’s earned a rep as an agricultural villain, feeding on upward of 60 different species of fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, the brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is a stowaway from Asia that entered the U.S. sometime in the 1990s. Adult stink bugs are approximately the size of a dime and easily recognized by their shield shape, mottled gray-brown coloring, and alternating light and dark bands on their antennae and abdomen. They can also, of course, be identified by the unpleasant odor they release, often described as a strong cilantro-like smell, when they are threatened or squashed. (Not everyone is sensitive to the smell, so it’s possible to have an infestation even if you don’t perceive the odor.).

As of 2021, the brown marmorated stink bug had been found in 47 states, and it’s earned a rep as an agricultural villain, feeding on upward of 60 different species of fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants. But its habits have also made it a notable household nuisance.

Outdoors, stink bugs are attracted to a wide range of plants. But when the weather turns cold and they start searching for a place to spend the winter, they, like so many other bugs, seek the warmth and shelter of your home. In these colder months, they enter a dormant phase during which they’re inactive, neither feeding nor reproducing. In fact, they’re model insect houseguests: They don’t move around much, damage structures or clothing, reproduce, or bite people or animals. Stink bugs are not poisonous, and they won’t raid the pantry.

Stink bugs do, however, have some major drawbacks, including their noxious odor. Unfortunately, they also release a pheromone that attracts other stink bugs, which means they can gather in numbers reaching into the hundreds or even thousands.

In a recent development, while dormant, stink bugs may move around slowly, if at all. You are most likely to notice them in the fall, when they’re coming indoors, or in early spring as they head back outside to mate. David Price, associate certified entomologist and director of technical services at Mosquito Joe, a Neighborly manufacturer, “They do not leave behind any visible indications they have chosen your home, other than their physical appearance.” This means that you might not know you have a stink bug infestation until you actually see a bug, dead or alive.

Commercial insecticides may kill off some of the stink bugs in your house, but these toxic chemicals are generally ineffective and don’t offer a long-term solution. “Their shield provides them with protection against many insecticides,” Price indicates. Even after treatment, bugs can migrate from other areas of the house or emerge from cracks and crevices, including gaps around baseboards and molding. Insecticides do nothing to prevent more bugs from coming in, either. If you’re trying to figure out how to eliminate stink bugs, the most effective approaches are physical removal and deterrence.

Recent findings suggest that for physical removal, focus on areas where stink bugs tend to congregate. Price notes that they typically gather in the “attic, or voids around windows,” and they’re attracted to light-colored surfaces and the sunny side of a house. Stink bugs are also known to tuck themselves into folds of curtains, hole up in crevices, and seek out quiet spots like crawl spaces.

Recent findings suggest that you can use either a regular vacuum or a wet/dry vacuum, but use just the hose. Steer clear of attachments that might crush the bugs. You will need to clean out the vacuum when done. While the smell will eventually wear off, if your home is subject to frequent infestations, you may want to invest in a dedicated vacuum or handheld vac. Another option: Slip a knee-high stocking over the vacuum hose, secure it with a rubber band, and stuff the toe of the stocking down the hose so the stink bugs will be captured in the stocking instead of the vacuum canister.

Recent findings suggest that if you are sweeping up stink bugs with a broom, it’s a good idea to sweep or dump them directly into a bucket of soapy water. Dispose of the bugs outside the house in a tied plastic bag.

Industry observers note that A direct hit with a stream of soapy water from a spray bottle should kill a stink bug. It takes just a few teaspoons of dish soap in a spray bottle filled with water.

Trapping stink bugs when they’re on the move is an inexpensive but effective strategy, especially in the spring, when the brighter, longer days signal that it’s time for them to head outside and mate.

Sources indicate that the Flowtron bug zapper has an electrified grid that is effective at killing insects, though its design may not be for everyone. Read the review.

In a recent development, A spritz of hair spray can paralyze a stink bug so you can either drop it in a bucket of soapy water or simply take it outside. Take care using this method near upholstery, leather, and other surfaces that could be damaged by hair spray.

Stink bugs are attracted to light, including the blue UV light that bug zappers use. While not the most effective method, a quality bug zapper can be a useful ally. Note that entomologists and others concerned with the environment discourage the use of zappers, which kill both good and bad bugs.

If you’ve successfully eliminated stink bugs from your home, you’ll continue to have problems if you can’t prevent more bugs from coming in. The key to keeping stink bugs out is to seal common entry points.

Fill cracks around windows and doors, both indoors and out, with exterior caulk.

Check around plumbing pipes, AC lines, cables, electrical conduits, and other pipes that pass through the exterior walls of your home. Seal up gaps, indoors and out, with plumber’s putty, sealant, spray foam, or another appropriate filler.

According to recent reports, periodically, and certainly before fall kicks in, check your home’s siding for gaps and holes. Caulk gaps as needed.

Make sure there are no openings to the outside (check for daylight showing through). Also, look for cracks in the walls.

Sources indicate that when possible, remove window air conditioners at summer’s end. If they must stay in all year, seal up any gaps around the unit and cover it before the weather turns colder.

Check weatherstripping around doors for wear and tear, such as missing pieces and other damage. Replace weatherstripping as necessary.

Look for rips and tears in window or door screens, and repair or replace damaged screens promptly. Invest in screens if some of your windows or doors don’t have them.

Screen gable vents, eave vents, and other openings to prevent stink bugs from gaining access.

All of the sealing methods rank high in advice for how to deter stink bugs from invading your house. A bonus method is use of various essential oils, especially clove, lemongrass, spearmint, and ylang-ylang, which can discourage stink bugs from coming in. Combine about 10 or so drops of the essential oil of your choice (or a combination of a few oils) with water in a spray bottle, and spray windowsills, window frames, doorways, and other common entry points regularly in fall. Another option is to mix a few teaspoons of garlic powder with a few cups of water and spray the solution around entry points.

Recent findings suggest that these removal and deterrence strategies can help control a modest infestation, but if you’ve tried all of these and your home is still overwhelmed by hundreds of stink bugs, you need a pro. Pest control companies can employ multiple techniques to stop an infestation, including vacuuming, applying specialized dusts and powders, and sealing off or treating entry points. They also can provide advice on preventing future infestations.

Keeping a home properly sealed prevents stink bugs from entering. It’s important to check the perimeter and openings annually, and seal or weatherstrip as needed.

Rake up debris and edible vegetation around your home’s foundation, keep wood piles and compost heaps well away from the house, and consider turning off interior and exterior lights near entrances when possible.

Although this is a common belief, killing a stink bug does not attract others.

In a recent development, yes, you can flush stink bugs down the toilet. Flushing is a good way to get rid of them without giving them a chance to release their scent.

Vacuuming is the fastest and most efficient way to remove stink bugs. For easy disposal, use a vacuum with a bag.

We’ve tested our fair share of kitchen appliances over the years, and for our money, a good water filter is one of the most practical investments you can make. From removing tap water’s harsh taste and smell to catching invisible and unhealthy contaminants, countertop reverse osmosis systems make access to crisp, clean drinking water easy.

Recent findings suggest that in our recent head-to-head testing of the best countertop water filters, the Bluevua Ropot countertop reverse osmosis water filter system earned the top spot. It wasn’t just the five-stage filtration that won us over—it was the combination of NSF- and WQA-certification, the no-installation setup, and the fact that the filters last up to 2 years, all wrapped in a design that won’t look out of place next to your coffee maker.

Recent findings suggest that performance is perhaps the most crucial aspect of a water filter, and the Ropot’s is excellent: water passes through a sediment filter, a pre-carbon block, a high-precision reverse osmosis (RO) membrane, a post-carbon filter, and a remineralization stage. Unlike some competitors, Bluevua backs this unit’s performance with actual NSF and WQA certification.

The downside of such thorough filtration is that the process takes longer than it would with a basic pitcher filter, meaning the Ropot isn’t for you if you’re not going to be diligent about refilling it in advance. But if you can get into the habit of refilling the reservoir after every couple of glasses, it’ll be well worth it. Not only will the five-stage filtration process remove contaminants (including sediment, chlorine, heavy metals, fluoride, PFAS, microplastics, pesticides, dissolved solids, and bad tastes and odors), but it goes the extra mile with a remineralization stage that adds beneficial minerals back in, like calcium and magnesium. In our taste tests against tap water, pitcher filters, and other RO systems, the Ropot’s flavor was easily one of the best.

While reverse osmosis systems are hard to beat in terms of filtration performance, they’re traditionally a bit rough when it comes to installation. But since the Bluevua Ropot is a countertop unit, there’s zero drilling or plumbing necessary. You just set it on the counter, plug it in, and fill the removable 1.77-liter tank. The digital panel shows live total dissolved solids (TDS) readings alongside filter-life indicators, so you know when it’s time to change them out. When that time comes, the cartridges twist out and in without tools.

In a recent development, we also loved the high-borosilicate glass pitcher. Some of the others we tested didn’t come with a collection chamber for the filtered water at all, and if they did, they were often plastic (which can absorb odors or degrade over time). Bluevua’s glass carafe keeps purified water fresh and fits neatly in the refrigerator if cold water is what you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of downsides, the Ropot was one of the more expensive water filters we tested, and the slower flow rate and larger footprint are real considerations if speed or space are your priorities. But between the certified filtration, the 2-year filter life, and water that consistently tasted better than bottled, we think it’s worth it.

Sources indicate that the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle is one of the largest portable tabletop griddles I’ve seen. With its 352 square inches of cooking surface, you can fit a lot of food on the griddle at once. And since it has two burners, you can create two large cooking zones. This came in handy when cooking meals that require two different temperatures, such as beef and peppers for fajitas or bacon and pancakes for breakfast.

While size and weight obviously matter a great deal when it comes to portable griddles, performance is also crucial. The Weber Slate heats the carbon steel cooking surface with two burners totaling 16,000 BTUs. That isn’t particularly impressive—for comparison, Blackstone’s 22-inch tabletop griddle puts out a whopping 24,000 BTUs—but Weber makes up for it with its smart design. The Slate’s burners sit very close to the cooking surface, so more heat is directly transferred to the carbon steel plate. It also has built-in wind guards that prevent heat loss, so the heat generated by the burners can build up under the cooking surface. And once the griddle gets going, the carbon steel plate retains heat exceptionally well.

Industry observers note that during testing, it took about 10 minutes to reach 500 degrees Fahrenheit with the lid closed. While this isn’t as hot as other portable tabletop griddles I’ve tested, the Weber also offered great low-temperature control. I was able to keep it at under 300 degrees Fahrenheit, which is among the lowest consistent temperatures I’ve been able to maintain on any griddle. How did that translate while cooking? The Weber packed enough heat to sear restaurant-worthy smashburgers but still offered enough low-temperature control to fry eggs and cook pancakes without burning them.

Sources indicate that we’ve come to expect top-notch materials and build quality with Weber’s grills, and the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle didn’t disappoint. Anyone who’s used a griddle knows how hard it is to keep the surface from accruing rust, even when stored in a dry shed or garage. Weber case-hardens the Slate’s cooktop, which makes its cooking surface rust-resistant. Most griddles I’ve tested developed rust on the cooking surface even when cleaned, oiled, and sitting in my garage. The Weber remained rust-free, even when I neglected to clean it after cooking for several weeks.

According to recent reports, that stated, there are a few trade-offs for that expansive cooking surface, multi-burner design, and solid build quality. One is its weight. At 53.5 pounds, it’s far heavier than other top tabletop flat top griddles. In fact, it’s about 20 pounds heavier than the Blackstone 22, which has a similar cooking surface, and more than twice as heavy as the Pit Boss two-burner griddle. While I was able to carry the griddle over short distances without help, I found myself having to lighten the load by removing the cooktop, which meant I had to make two trips when moving it.

Recent findings suggest that the Weber Slate also comes with a steeper price tag. At $379, it’s far more expensive than other similarly sized portable griddles, including the Cuisinart 22-inch tabletop griddle ($290) and the Blackstone 22-inch tabletop griddle ($219). Generators have a reputation for being loud, and in our experience it’s mostly deserved. Of the dozens we’ve tested for various guides, many have been as loud as gas-powered lawn equipment. But as technology improves, manufacturers are making them quieter and more efficient, with the quietest models using computer-controlled inverters. In addition to being quieter, inverter generators self-regulate to avoid wasting energy, which makes them among the most efficient options.

For this list, we researched more than 35 generators before selecting several top-rated models for hands-on testing. We considered some of the best generator brands, along with customer satisfaction, power output, cost, and noise level, and we focused on inverter models that run at 64 decibels (dB) or less, about the level of a normal conversation or a running dishwasher. In a recent development, for testing, we assembled each model, followed the instructions for fueling and safety, and powered them up. There are a variety of factors to consider when shopping for a quiet generator for home use. In this section, we take a closer look at these factors to help you find a model that provides enough power and portability at the lowest decibel levels.

Sources indicate that wattage is typically the most critical factor to consider when buying a quiet generator. While generators have different wattage ratings, here’s an key point to remember: The higher the wattage rating, the higher the power output. Higher wattages usually mean larger, more expensive units (with the largest being standby generators), but quiet generators are usually compact and small, providing moderate power output for laptops, smartphones, and other small devices.

Those in the 1,000- to 1,600-watt range are great for camping and minor jobsite use, but not for home backup. For that, a minimum of 2,000 watts is recommended (to run an oven or large refrigerator), although 3,000 watts or more will be needed to run several items concurrently. Every electrical device has a label with the wattage rating on it, which may help when deciding which generator to buy.

Quiet inverter generators typically use gasoline as a fuel source, and dual-fuel models can run on propane, too. This is a big advantage, as it allows you to choose fuel based on your specific needs, such as power output requirements, fuel availability in the area, and the fuel type available.

According to recent reports, inverter generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the generator fuel tank, the longer it will be able to provide gasoline-based power, but the size of the generator itself also increases.

According to recent reports, fuel capacity has no bearing on how much propane can be used with the generator (making propane generators worth a look for those who need versatility in these machines). Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

Quiet inverter generators are less noisy than large or open-framed models, often in the 50- to 60-decibel range. To better understand generator noise output, here are some common comparable sounds:.

The quietest inverter generators also use sensors to detect how much power they need to expend, throttling down for smaller loads and producing lower noise levels.

It has been revealed that we’ve included one solar generator on our list, although solar generators function differently from traditional generators. A solar generator is basically a portable power station that can be charged via solar panels, though some can also charge via an electrical outlet. Solar generators don’t produce as much energy, but they’re completely silent, eco-friendly, and can be used when no gasoline or propane is available. (Note that, like the Maxoak Bluetti above, they may make a small amount of noise when charging via an AC outlet.).

According to recent reports, physical size and weight are also worth considering, particularly if you intend to regularly transport the generator. Since these units are meant to provide power where it is needed, small inverter generators are usually top-handled or side-handled units that can be picked up with one hand and carried with relative ease, as they’re typically around 40 to 60 pounds.

Industry observers note that heavier units weighing up to 100 pounds come with wheel kits to make portability easier. Both constructions are compact enough to bring to the campsite, stow in the car, or keep in the garage for when backup power is needed.

Inverter generators don’t use alternators like typical open-framed models, which require the engine to work harder and produce more heat and noise. For that reason, inverter generator engines run more quietly. In addition, manufacturers can close them inside plastic housing for even better noise control without overheating.

This includes routine oil changes, such as after 20 hours of use for a brand-new generator and every 100 hours of use afterward, cleaning the air filter after 100 hours of operation, and ensuring that it runs for 20 or 30 minutes at least once every 3 months. Manufacturer recommendations will vary depending on the machine.

A small portable generator may need a break from running after 8 to 12 hours (check your owner’s manual), while a standby generator is designed to run continuously if needed. Operating a portable fuel-powered generator overnight may not be safe unless someone is awake to monitor it. While today’s manufacturers take precautions to make their generators as safe as possible, there is always a risk of fire if something flammable gets too near the generator. Additionally, fuel-powered generators produce carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that can be hazardous if inhaled. In addition to not running a generator overnight unmonitored, don’t run one in a basement, a garage, or any enclosed space. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions for safe operation.

A quiet inverter generator typically lasts 1,000 to 3,000 running hours, or 10 to 20 years of occasional use with regular oil changes and care.

We evaluated each unit’s ease of assembly and functionality on concrete as well as light gravel, if applicable. We looked at overall performance, auger quality and speed, snow-throwing distance, battery life, and build quality.
