After rating each unit based on the above factors, we assigned awards to worthy models.

Recent findings suggest that compared to traditional two-stage machines, single-stage snow blowers are lighter, more mobile, and better suited to light- to moderate-duty jobs. For folks who regularly get severe storms with several feet of heavy snow at a time, these machines might be underpowered.

However, if you’re looking for a good snow blower that can clear smaller amounts of snow on average-size driveways and walkways, a single-stage model will be a relatively cheap snow blower that still offers plenty of convenience power.

According to recent reports, according to Wes Bollingmo, Channel & Product Support Manager at Toro, one of the most important things to consider when choosing a snow blower is its type, and that doesn’t mean gas or electric. Wes claims, “While fuel types do matter in the buying process, it’s much more important to ensure you have the proper type of snow blower: single-stage, in-line two-stage, or two-stage.” After that, you can look into things like power source, clearing width and depth, ease of use, and additional features.

The best snow blowers come in corded electric, battery-powered, and gas-powered varieties.

Toro’s Wes Bollingmo does point out, however, that the power difference between gas and electric machines is becoming less substantial over time. “Thanks to recent technological advances, today’s battery-powered snow blowers offer performance comparable to gas models, making fuel type less of a deciding factor than in years past,” he notes. Still, since power source can impact ease of use, it remains a relevant consideration.

Weight plays a significant role in how easy it is to push or turn a snow blower. Though a large snow blower can clear a driveway in fewer passes than a small snow blower, bigger machines are harder to maneuver.

It has been revealed that most single-stage gas snow blowers weigh at least 80 to 100 pounds, while corded and cordless blowers weigh closer to 30 to 60 pounds. Those needing something lighter may want to consider a handheld snow blower, snow thrower, or electric shovel snow blower.

Before choosing the best single-stage snow blower, it’s important to consider the width and depth of snow the machine can clear with each pass. Most single-stage machines can clear paths between 15 and 22 inches wide—and the wider the path, the faster you’re finished.

Intake height determines the depth of snow each tool can remove with each pass, and most single-stage snow blowers have an intake depth between 7 and 12 inches. A good rule of thumb is to choose a snow blower with an intake depth 2 inches higher than your area’s average snowfall.

Wheeled snow blowers feature two large rear wheels that drive the machine forward, while tracked models have tracks similar to those found on a military tank.

Sources indicate that terrain type will influence which of these design options is best for a specific user. Paved surfaces, such as driveways and sidewalks, are best suited for wheeled snow blowers. Tracked snow blowers are better suited for unpaved surfaces. Grade also has a significant impact; steep driveways require a snow blower with good traction and enough power to pull it up a snow-covered slope.

Speed control in a snow blower can refer to both the speed at which you can move the machine as well as the speed of the auger. Gas snow blowers can be quite heavy, so many shoppers prefer self-propelled models to make pushing them faster and easier. Battery-powered blowers are generally lighter and feature digital drive systems that help optimize output without unnecessary effort.Blowers with variable-speed augers can be useful for adapting to different types of snow. If the snowfall is nice and light, increasing the speed at which the snow is scooped and thrown through the chute will make it easier to move the machine. For heavy, packed snow, you will need to slow the blower to give the machine time to discharge it without clogging.

Sources indicate that the chute, a curved, hollow tube that extends from the back of the intake on a snow blower, provides a route for the snow to be thrown from the machine. On most blowers, a manual crank or lever lets owners change the angle and direction of the snow being displaced.

Premium snow blowers, however, have auto-rotating chutes that consumers turn by pushing a button near the handle, which doesn’t require the machine to be stopped. The angle on some chutes also can be changed to allow the snow blower to throw snow even further.

Single-stage snow blowers often boast some extra features to improve ease of use.

We asked Corey Welch, founder and CEO of Mow & Snow, an on-demand snow removal and lawn care company in Canada, which of these features he appreciates most on a snow blower. He said, “Headlights are a game-changer for early mornings or late evenings, and heated handles are a luxury that keeps your hands from freezing during long jobs.” Anyone looking to increase comfort and ease of use will want to look for a model with these features.

If you still have questions about single-stage snow blowers, we suggest you refer to the answers to common FAQs below before putting on your work boots and heading outside.

The biggest difference between a single-stage vs. a two-stage snow blower is power. Most single-stage snow blowers can handle a maximum of 7 to 12 inches of snow, whereas two-stage snow blowers can tackle up to 2 feet. The “stage” term refers to how each blower removes snow. A single-stage snow blower has an auger that both gathers and blows away the snow. A two-stage snow blower, in comparison, has an auger that sucks up the snow and an impeller that rolls out it into the air. In addition to being able to remove deeper snow, two-stage snow blowers also have larger intakes that range in width from 20 to 36 inches.

According to recent reports, the length of the extension cord depends on the gauge of the power cable. A 12-gauge cord will work up to 100 feet, while a slimmer 14-gauge cord only extends about 50 feet.

It has been revealed that getting a snow blower started depends on its power source. Keep these tips in mind for electric and gas-powered machines: – Corded electric: Plug the unit into an outlet and press the start button. These models take their power from an AC power source, so there are no concerns with low-temperature start-ups. – Cordless electric: Some electric snow blowers will not start if the battery is too cold. It’s a good idea to store lithium-ion batteries at room temperature to prevent this glitch. – Gas-powered: Gas snow blowers with a pull-start motor may be challenging to start in low temperatures. Make sure to use lightweight motor oil, such as 5W-30, which is designed to operate at low temperatures.

Industry observers note that periodically changing the fuel filter ensures contaminants won’t find their way inside the engine and negatively impact performance. The fuel filter is usually located between the fuel pump and fuel tank. Change the filter by removing the two hoses that connect to it, making sure to keep the hoses pointing upward to prevent fuel from leaking out of the tank. Install the latest filter by attaching the hoses to the line leading from the fuel tank and the line leading to the engine.

A single-stage snow blower might use gas, corded electricity, or a battery as its fuel.

Sources indicate that yes, single-stage snow blowers are good, though they aren’t right for everyone. If you live in an area with light to medium amounts of snowfall and don’t have an especially large property, a single-stage snow blower can provide effective performance and affordability.

According to recent reports, the augers on single-stage snow blowers are designed to clear snow down to the ground, so using them on grass is not recommended. They may damage your lawn or even pick up debris that can damage your machine.

Sources indicate that before purchasing a snow blower for a gravel driveway, it’s vital to understand that not all machines will work for this type of surface. For example, most single-stage snow blowers and electric snow shovels have augers that scrape along the ground. While this design is great for snow removal from smooth pavement, sidewalks, and heated driveways, it doesn’t work well on gravel driveways since it will pick up gravel in addition to snow.

Sources indicate that still, there’s no need to resort to using a standard snow shovel. Two-stage and three-stage snow blowers have augers that operate an inch or so above the ground as well as adjustable skids that provide clearance to prevent the machine from scooping up gravel.

Understanding which types of snow blowers are suitable for gravel driveways and which are not is the first step in selecting the right model. Ahead, learn more about the three types of snow blowers as well as other important features, such as power output and intake width.

Recent findings suggest that there are three main types of snow blowers: single-stage, two-stage, and three-stage. Each one clears snow a bit differently, but for gravel driveways, two-stage models are ideal. Here’s how each of these snow blowers works.

Like all snow blowers, a single-stage snow blower or snow thrower uses an auger with serrated metal blades to scoop snow and launch it through the chute. Since the auger on this type of snow blower skims along the ground, it’s an excellent option for smooth pavement but a poor choice for loose gravel. If used on a gravel driveway, a single-stage snow blower will gather and throw rocks along with snow.

Similar to a single-stage snow blower, a two-stage model uses an auger to pull snow into the chute. However, rather than use the force of the auger to launch the snow, two-stage snow blowers rely on large impeller fans to propel the snow out of the chute. In addition to being able to throw snow much farther than a single-stage model, a two-stage snow blower’s auger does not come into contact with the ground. Instead of resting on the auger, the snow blower glides on two adjustable skid pads—a design that makes a two-stage model ideal for gravel surfaces.

According to recent reports, this heavy-duty snow blower uses an auger and impeller fan along with an accelerator, which is  a corkscrew-shaped blade that sits perpendicular to the auger and pulls snow quickly into the machine as it spins. True to its name, an accelerator allows the machine to glide more quickly through snow. These powerful snow blowers can throw snow up to 50 feet away and have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide. This makes them ideal for covering large driveways. Like a two-stage snow blower, a three-stage model’s auger does not touch the ground, so it’s a good choice for gravel surfaces. Three-stage blowers also come with a hefty price tag. As such, they are typically only needed for regions that see very heavy snowfall.

When selecting a snow blower, consider how much power it needs to get the job done. Snow blowers have either a gas engine or, with battery-powered models, an electric motor. A gas snow blower’s power is measured in cubic centimeters. The higher the cc, the better able the snow blower is to move through deeper snow and the farther it can launch it. Two-stage snow blowers for gravel driveways have engines ranging between 200cc and 250cc.

Industry observers note that electric snow blowers generally use two batteries to maximize runtime, though many can run on one battery (but they won’t run as long). Total runtime varies depending on the voltage and amp hours of the batteries, the number of batteries used, and, of course, the amount and type of snow being cleared. Depending on these factors, many battery-powered snow blowers can run for between 30 and 70 minutes. Some electric snow blowers also have an additional port that enables adding a third battery to extend runtime.

According to recent reports, although battery-powered snow blowers may not be quite as powerful as gas-powered options, they operate at a much lower noise level and don’t produce exhaust fumes. They also don’t require periodic oil changes, making snow blower maintenance easier. Just keep in mind that lithium-ion batteries typically only last 3 to 6 years before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge, at which point they need to be replaced. Still, even replacing batteries may be less expensive than paying the cost of snow removal in areas that receive regular snowfall.

According to recent reports, the width of the snow blower refers to the size of its intake and determines how broad a swath of snow the machine can remove with each pass. Most single-stage snow blowers remove snow in 11- to 22-inch swaths with each pass, making them suitable for small driveways and walks. Two-stage models range in width from 22 to 30 inches, making them ideal for most driveways. Large three-stage snow blowers have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide.

Some of the best snow blowers for gravel driveways may come equipped with other useful features that make them easier and, in some cases, safer to use, such as:.

In addition to buying a snow blower rated to work on gravel surfaces, there are other measures you can take to improve performance when clearing snow from this type of surface.

First and foremost, ensure the skid shoes—the two metal pieces that raise the snow blower intake and auger above the ground—are properly adjusted so that the intake is about 1 inch off the ground. This gap will provide enough clearance between the auger and the ground to prevent it from contacting the gravel.

If dealing with snow deeper than the height of the auger, consider raising the skid shoes to their highest setting to get the top layer of snow, then lower it to remove the remaining snow.

According to recent reports, in windy conditions, start blowing upwind on the driveway and set the chute to discharge snow downwind. If the snow is particularly wet, adding nonstick snow blower spray to the chute can help prevent clogging.

When finished, make sure to clear any remaining snow from the auger to prevent it from freezing and clogging the intake.

The best way to remove snow from a gravel driveway is to adjust the snow blower’s skid shoes to elevate its intake above the ground. This will prevent the machine from picking up and throwing gravel. If you don’t have a snow blower for your gravel driveway yet, check out our guide on clever hacks for how to shovel snow.

The best kind of snow blower to use on gravel is a two-stage model. The auger on a single-stage snow blower makes contact with the ground, so it will pick up gravel and throw it. A two-stage or three-stage snow blower has an intake that is elevated above the ground, allowing it to pick up snow without disturbing the gravel beneath it. Three-stage models work similarly, but they are heavy-duty options generally used by professionals.

They can last 10 years or many more if properly cared for. Snow blower maintenance includes changing the oil (for gas-powered models); lubricating the axle and augers; and periodically checking the shear pins, skid shoes, and belts for wear. Electric snow blowers require battery replacement about every 3 years if used regularly or up to 6 years if used intermittently.

The best time to get a good price on a snow blower is in either May or June, when manufacturers are introducing latest models and demand for these winter-weather machines is low. If you need to buy outside this period, our guide on the best cheap snow blowers offers some excellent options.

Industry observers note that we asked Thomas Vanneli, founder and CEO of Minneapolis, Minnesota’s Tomms Property Solutions, for advice on this problem. He mentioned, “To avoid scratching concrete, rubber or polymer skid shoes should be installed. Skid shoes stop the metal from coming into contact with the concrete, which will protect it from dings and scratches.” You can also prevent damage to concrete surfaces by adjusting the skid shoes so the intake sits about an inch off the ground.

Sometimes, updating a room can be as simple as updating the window treatments for a quick facelift. The right choice can give you a sleek, modern aesthetic or a softer, more inviting atmosphere. But it’s not all just looks, they also control natural light, maintain privacy, and can even improve your home’s energy efficiency.

Sources indicate that blinds and shades are the two popular options, each with their own advantages in interior design and function. So, which one is right for your space? From design preferences and trends to the practical things like maintenance and insulation, we’ll take a look at the pros and cons of blinds vs. shades to help you find the perfect fit for your home.

Sources indicate that shades and blinds are both hung within (or just outside) the top of a window frame, and extend to the bottom of the glass pane, but the window coverings differ in the way they’re constructed. Blinds are composed of individual slats made from hard materials like wood, aluminum, or vinyl. These slats can be tilted to control the amount and direction of sunlight entering a room. Most blinds can also be raised or pulled to the side to fully expose the window.

Window shades, on the other hand, are generally made from a continuous piece of fabric or another flexible material that rolls, folds, or stacks when raised. They give a softer appearance and come in a variety of styles, from light-filtering roller shades to insulating cellular shades.

Blinds.com’s blackout cellular shade provides privacy and insulation; customize it as motorized, top down/bottom up, or corded/cordless.

Blinds and shades have their own advantages, so there isn’t an outright winner for every home. Blinds give you more control over light and privacy, while shades can look softer and have insulating properties. Here’s a breakdown of the pros and cons of each.

The right window treatment depends on more than just how they look. Before deciding between blinds and shades, consider how you use the room, how much natural light you want, and how much maintenance you’re willing to take on. These key factors can help narrow down your options.

Blinds and shades will both provide privacy, but they each do it differently. Blinds give you more flexibility throughout the day. You can angle the slats to block the view from outside without completely closing off the light from the window. This makes them practical for living rooms, home offices, and other spaces where you want some natural light without feeling exposed.

Recent findings suggest that shades give you privacy when they’re lowered, but the amount of privacy will depend on the fabric. Sheer and light-filtering materials can provide privacy during the day, but will show silhouettes at night when your lights are on. Room-darkening and blackout shades are better for bedrooms and bathrooms, where privacy is definitely a must.

Blinds.com’s premium roller shade blocks UV rays and preserves views, and is available in a variety of patterns, colors, and fabrics.

Sources indicate that for precise control over how much sunlight gets through the window, blinds have the upper hand. The adjustable slats let you redirect sunlight up at the ceiling or away from a TV or computer screen, reducing glare while still keeping some natural light.

Sources indicate that shades are different. Light-filtering fabrics soften the harsh sunlight and give a gentle glow, while blackout shades are designed to block most incoming light. That noted, shades don’t really let you fine-tune as much as blinds. For more flexibility, try top-down/bottom-up shades, which can be lowered from the top or raised from the bottom, or dual shades that use both light-filtering and blackout materials.

Cost for both blinds and shades will depend on the materials, size, and additional features. Basic vinyl or aluminum blinds tend to be the most budget-friendly options, so they’re practical if you’re looking to cover multiple windows without spending a fortune.

Recent findings suggest that shades can also be affordable, assuming you’re looking at simple roller shades made from synthetic fabrics. However, premium Roman shades, double-cell cellular shades, and custom fabric options will cost more.

In a recent development, for either option, custom sizing, professional installation, and motorized or smart controls can significantly inflate the price tag. Standard-sized, manually operated window treatments are usually the cheapest choice.

Sources indicate that window treatments can also help keep your home comfortable throughout the year. When it comes to insulation, however, certain types of shades have a clear advantage.

According to recent reports, cellular shades are particularly effective thanks to their honeycomb construction, which traps air in pockets between the window and the room. This helps reduce heat loss during winter and heat gain during summer, potentially lowering your energy bills. Roman shades with insulating liners can also provide some thermal benefits.

Sources indicate that blinds can help reduce solar heat gain by blocking or redirecting direct sunlight, but gaps between the slats don’t give you much insulation. If energy efficiency is one of your priorities, well-fitted cellular shades may be your best bet.

Older blinds and shades have long pull or loop cords, which are a serious strangulation hazard to young children and pets. Luckily, today’s options are much safer, with cordless designs becoming the standard for both blinds and shades.

Sources indicate that there was even an update to window-covering safety standards in June 2024, which restricted hazardous cords on custom window coverings even more. Thanks to this change, you can now choose from a wide range of cordless and motorized options in both categories.

According to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, cordless window coverings are the safest choice for homes with young children. If you still have older cord-operated blinds or shades, replacing them with cordless alternatives is recommended.

These fabric vertical blinds from Blinds.com filter harsh sunlight and are durable, cost-effective alternatives to drapes.

Window treatments can have a surprising impact on the look and feel of a room. If you’re wondering how to dress a window without curtains, both blinds and shades give you plenty of stylish options. Blinds have a structured, tailored appearance that works well in modern, minimalist, and traditional interiors. Wood and faux wood blinds can add warmth and natural texture, while aluminum blinds look great in industrial or modern spaces.

Shades have a little more variety in terms of fabric, color, pattern, and texture. Roman shades can create an elegant, layered look, while simple roller shades are ideal for a clean, understated aesthetic. Woven wood shades made from bamboo or other natural materials can give organic texture and complement coastal, bohemian, or rustic spaces.

Of course, it will all come down to your own preference and the atmosphere you’re trying to create. Blinds are ideal for a crisp, structured look, while shades can make a room feel softer and more inviting.

In general, blinds are easier to maintain than shades. The hard surfaces are easy to dust or wipe down with a damp cloth, so they’re a great choice for kitchens, bathrooms, and other areas where moisture or splashes are common. Just keep in mind, though, that cleaning each individual slat can take time.

Fabric shades need a gentler approach. Most can be vacuumed with a brush attachment, while certain materials can be spot-cleaned. More delicate fabrics may need professional cleaning, and exposure to sunlight can cause some materials to fade over time.

In a busy house, low-maintenance blinds or easy-clean roller shades may be the most practical options.

Shades come in a huge range of styles, from simple designs to decorative options that can be more of a focal point in the room. Some of the most popular types include:.

According to recent reports, when choosing between blinds and shades, the decision comes down to what you want in your space. If precise light control, durability, and easy cleaning are your priorities, blinds are probably best. If you prefer a softer aesthetic, better insulation, or room darkening, shades may be worth the extra cost.

According to recent reports, remember, you don’t have to commit to one type of window treatments and use it throughout the home. Use blinds for high-traffic areas like kitchens and home offices, and shades for bedrooms and living spaces where comfort and aesthetics are more of a priority. Mixing and matching window treatments can help you strike the right balance between style, functionality, and budget.

#8771. Is Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Premised Upon a "Misquote"? (Updated)

Is Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Premised Upon a "Misquote"? (Updated)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This past week, the Upcoming York Times published an article by Mike McIntire and Eli Murray alleging that a "pivotal legal test" for determining whether gun control laws are constitutional is "based on a misquote." Yet it appears it is the NYT's reporters who misfired.
  • When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court's own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both "dangerous and unusual.".
  • For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past week, the Upcoming York Times published an article by Mike McIntire and Eli Murray alleging that a "pivotal legal test" for determining whether gun control laws are constitutional is "based on a misquote." Yet it appears it is the NYT's reporters who misfired.

Here is the article's basic claim:.

When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court's own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both "dangerous and unusual.".

For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws. It is a pivotal legal test.

It is also based on a misquote.

In a recent development, justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in the 2008 case, District of Columbia v. Heller, attributed the "dangerous and unusual" language to Sir William Blackstone, an 18th-century English jurist whose writings became the basis for much of American law.

But in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

But is there actually an error in the opinion? Here is the paragraph from Heller in which the alleged misquotation occurs, with the allegedly offending sentence underlined:.

Industry observers note that we also recognize another key limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller said, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons." See 4 Blackstone 148–149 (1769); 3 B. Wilson, Works of the Honourable James Wilson 79 (1804); J. Dunlap, The Latest-York Justice 8 (1815); C. Humphreys, A Compendium of the Common Law in Force in Kentucky 482 (1822); 1 W. Russell, A Treatise on Crimes and Indictable Misdemeanors 271–272 (1831); H. Stephen, Summary of the Criminal Law 48 (1840); E. Lewis, An Abridgment of the Criminal Law of the United States 64 (1847); F. Wharton, A Treatise on the Criminal Law of the United States 726 (1852). See also State v. Langford, 10 N. C. 381, 383–384 (1824); O'Neill v. State, 16 Ala. 65, 67 (1849); English v. State, 35 Tex. 473, 476 (1871); State v. Lanier, 71 N. C. 288, 289 (1874).

Sources indicate that note that the claim, with the quotation, is followed by a "See" string cite (followed, in turn, by a "See also" string cite of further authorities). If they were at all familiar with how legal citation works, this should have given the NYT reporters pause. As others have noted, the Supreme Court's style guide indicates that the "see" signal is not used for direct quotations. Rather it indicates that "the cited authority is basic source material supporting, although not stating, the text proposition" (emphasis added). Blackstone is cited first not because it is the dominant source but because the authorities are listed in chronological order.

What makes matters worse is that it appears the authors of the story were informed of all this before the story went to press. One of the story authors contacted John Bash, who clerked for Justice Antonin Scalia the term Heller was decided and worked on the case, and Bash explained all of this to the reporter, as Bash details in this LinkedIn post. Bash writes:.

According to recent reports, this is stunning. A recent article in The Upcoming York Times claims that District of Columbia v. Heller--the 2008 Supreme Court case holding that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to own a firearm--contains a "misquote" of Blackstone. The supposed misquote is the phrase "dangerous and unusual weapons" in this passage:.

We also recognize another vital limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller said, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons.".

According to recent reports, that passage is followed by the signal "See" and numerous citations, the first of which is Blackstone. The Blackstone source claims "dangerous or unusual weapons" ("or" instead of "and"), but a number of the sources that follow say "dangerous and unusual weapons," in addition to sources that use the Blackstone disjunctive framing.

Back in October the New York Times reporter reached out to me about this, presumably because I was the law clerk for Justice Scalia on Heller. I immediately wrote back with a full on-the-record explanation of why there was no misquote. Yet the article does not refer to my explanation at all and asserts with no qualification that it was a misquote.

Sources indicate that so if anyone is interested, I have posted my email below verbatim. I will also put in the comments my follow-up when the reporter asked me a question.

Here is the e-mail Bash sent to the reporter working on the story:.

Hi Mike, thanks for reaching out on this.

Even if I remembered any conversation with Justice Scalia about this particular point (which I don't), it would not be ethical for me to share private conversations I had during my clerkship wth Justice Scalia about the substance of opinions.

In a recent development, but just as an appellate lawyer, I don't see the glitch. If the historical sources are mixed on the conjunctive or disjunctive framing, then it is true that there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual, the narrower category that is encompassed by either framing. The fact that Blackstone is the first citation is just because the treatise citations are in chronological order (consistent with making a point about historical tradition), followed by case citations also in chronological order. The introduction of the treatise list with a "See" signal (rather than no signal) means that the quoted phrase is not necessarily a direct quote from each source (or any source)—as with the "See also" signal for the cases. And assuming that it's correct that the conjunctive sources all trace back to a single 18th Century treatise, that would not detract from the point that learned commentators had endorsed or applied that test through early American history, which is the point the text is making about historical tradition.

Here is the first follow-up e-mail Bash sent "in response to the reporter asking if he could quote me and whether the opinion purposefully omitted the Hawkins treatise quoted in the conjunctive-framing sources so that Blackstone would be first":.

Sources indicate that sure. Happy to take a look at the quote.

Industry observers note that can't speak to the thinking that went into the opinion, but I really doubt that. As I mentioned earlier, I don't think the provenance of the limitation is particularly relevant; the point was that commentators had recognized it throughout history. For example, in a Fourth Amendment case, a court might make the point that the curtilage rule—that the immediate vicinity of the home is considered part of the home—has been recognized through American history, citing late Eighteenth Century and Nineteenth Century treatises and cases. Even if that rule could be traced back to a single uncited treatise, that's not really the point. It's that courts and commentators endorsed it and so that history and tradition informs the constitutional analysis.

It has been revealed that and all that aside, I just think it is implausible that the paragraph would be understood differently if Blackstone had been the second citation rather than the first—especially since Hawkins was himself a very influential legal commentator (if I recall correctly). I've never heard of a court or litigant attributing weight to the order of sources subject to the same signal (e.g., "See"), which would seem to me especially unwarranted when the sources are presented chronologically (and so there is an obvious explanation for the ordering other than importance). As I noted before, I think all the sources together make clear a uniform historical tradition of prohibiting dangerous and unusual weapons, the category encompassed by all of their articulations of the rule.

Interestingly enough, the NYT article concludes citing a scholar affirming Bash's contention that, as the relevant passage claims, "there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual," or as some would put it, those arms that are "unusually dangerous." Insofar as some lower courts have applied a different analysis, it is not clear to me how that is attributable to Scalia's language in Heller, or the contested passage.

The NYT story ends citing a scholar for the proposition that "relying on centuries-old legal precedents requires understanding how earlier generations used language." One might conclude that those writing on the Supreme Court should heed a similar admonition.

PATCH: The NYT has issued this response to criticism of the article:.

In a recent development, the Times's article reported that Justice Scalia wrongly attributed the direct quote "dangerous and unusual" to Blackstone. That is a fact, and one that has also been recognized by a federal appeals court. This reporting is an accurate portrayal of what Justice Scalia did.

It has been revealed that in the Heller opinion, Justice Scalia chose to put the conjunctive phrase "dangerous and unusual" in direct quotes, and per legal style, citations for direct quotes should reflect the exact wording. Instead, he used a "see" signal to introduce 12 sources, only half of which were conjunctive. The rest, including Blackstone, used the disjunctive "dangerous or unusual.".

Industry observers note that following that, the result of the decision was to create a conjunctive doctrine that has since been inaccurately credited to Blackstone in hundreds of court briefs and opinions--including at the Supreme Court. Justice Clarence Thomas in a 2020 dissent wrote: "Sir William Blackstone concluded the Statute of Northampton banned only the carrying of 'dangerous and unusual weapons.'" He cited the Heller opinion as his source.

The article also highlights that there has been a debate over this language in the centuries since Blackstone's writing, how the language was used in Heller and how it's been used since.

It seems to me the Times is still not accounting for the meaning of the "see" signal, but readers can judge for themselves whether the Times has substantiated the broad claim made by the original article.

SECOND PATCH: After John Bash's initial LinkedIn post, one of the Times reporters reached out with a defense of the story. The reporter's message was "off the record," but here was Bash's reply.

There is obviously, at minimum, a substantial argument that it was not a misquote, especially given the ordinary use of the signal "see" and the fact that numerous sources come after. I don't understand how a straight news article, as opposed to an opinion piece, could state definitively that it is a "misquote" with no explanation of the contrary point of view, or even a modifier like "arguably" or "potentially."  The fact that judicial opinions sometimes use "See" unnecessarily does not detract from the basic meaning of that signal: Bluebook Signals Explained ("See indicates that the source clearly, though indirectly, supports a proposition. That is, the source does not directly state your proposition, but if a reader checked the source, it would be immediately clear to her that it supports your proposition."). And the fact that you didn't use quotes from people "on the other side" is irrelevant when the article exclusively articulates their point of view, as a fact no less.

More importantly, the article entirely omits that the historical point the sentence was making—that it has long been understood that "dangerous and unusual weapons" can be prohibited—is fully supported by sources that articulate either that specific framing or the broader disjunctive framing that encompasses the specific framing. Your statement that the Court's citation is "wrong" is simply not correct. The sentence does not say that Blackstone articulated a conjunctive formulation. It notes that there was an historical tradition of prohibiting "dangerous and unusual weapons."  Every cited source supports that proposition. And that is why "see" is used—the inference from the sources in their totality is that there was a tradition of prohibiting certain types of arms, even though none of the sources themselves specifically addresses the question of tradition.

It seems to me that a fair presentation would have laid this out for the readers and let them decide, rather than simply asserting that it was a misquote.

Caulk fixes myriad projects around the house, from outdoor maintenance to indoor decorating. What makes the material such a versatile DIY essential? The rubbery substance, available in a variety of formulations, including silicone, latex, acrylic, butyl rubber, polyurethane, and construction adhesives, can bond to almost any material, making it a wonderfully flexible material for projects indoors and out. With the right tube of caulk, you can solve just about any problem—including these common issues.

Caulking windows and doors is the best way to reduce drafts, cut home energy costs, enhance your house’s energy efficiency, and decrease your carbon footprint, according to the Consumer Federation of America. For this job, choose either acrylic latex or vinyl latex caulk. Acrylic latex caulk works best in dry environments and will perform well for up to 15 years, while vinyl latex can be used in damp areas and lasts about 5 years.

Sources indicate that concrete and mortar repair caulk is an excellent tool for sealing cracks and gaps in concrete, brick, stucco, stone, and metal. Similarly, it’s perfect for repairing small fissures in foundations and basement walls that allow insects, rodents, and other pests to enter your home. Designed for both interior and exterior use, concrete and mortar repair caulk has a textured finish and can be painted once it’s dry.

No matter how carefully you measure and cut, you often end up with little gaps between, above, and below moldings and baseboards. When you need to close the gap, acrylic latex caulk is one of the best caulks for baseboards, ideal for filling in those small spaces. The product dries quickly and can be painted as soon as 6 to 8 hours after application. Acrylic latex also comes in a variety of different pigments, so you can match the color to the surrounding material.

Industry observers note that over time, small spaces can open up between tiles, and in moist environments that’s an invitation for mold and mildew to grow behind the walls. Both 100 percent silicone caulk and siliconized acrylic caulk are ideal for wet environments and form a durable, watertight seal. Mold- and mildew-resistant silicone caulk is made for nonporous surfaces like ceramic, glass, and metal, while waterproof siliconized acrylic caulk works well on tubs, tile, glass, and ceramic tile surfaces. Gorilla silicone sealant is ideal to use since it is waterproof, and mold and mildew resistant.

According to recent reports, gorilla silicone caulk is flexible, adheres well, and creates a mold- and mildew-resistant barrier on bathroom surfaces. Read the review.

When you need to cover small holes and tiny cracks prior to painting, painter’s caulk, an acrylic latex compound, is just what you need. Painter’s caulk such as DAP Alex painter’s caulk adheres to wood, drywall, masonry, and other surfaces. Because it dries to a paintable texture in about an hour, it’s a good choice for busy DIYers.

It has been revealed that fire barrier sealant, a specialized type of caulk, does more than patch holes. It actually helps make your home safer by preventing fire from moving through open spaces within a structure. Fire barrier sealant can be used to seal holes, gaps, and cracks around holes in interior framing, especially around plumbing or electrical conduits.

Industry observers note that when a length of molding falls off, a corner of carpet comes up, or a tile comes loose, all-purpose caulk can often fix it. Dab a little caulk behind the loose piece, then stick it back into place. You can even use an all-purpose caulk like GE all-purpose silicone caulk to install wood wall paneling without nails.

Sources indicate that to keep wallpaper from pulling up as it dries, run caulk along all trimmed paper seams, especially in the corners, then smooth with a wet sponge or finger to remove any surface imperfections. For wallpaper that is peeling, lift up the loose section of paper, apply adhesive under it, then smooth the paper back against the wall. Once the adhesive dries, apply a continuous bead of caulk along the seam to keep it from peeling up again.

It has been revealed that with the right caulk, you can even repair a roof! Roof repair caulk, like Roofers Choice Roof Cement Caulk, can be used to seal small cracks or gaps along roof edges, between shingles, and around skylights or flashing. As you might expect, roof repair caulk is completely weatherproof and waterproof, and can be used in wet areas or on dry surfaces.

Industry observers note that as your home’s gutters age, they can develop cracks and gaps, especially around joints and downspout junctions. Butyl rubber caulk, a strong waterproof sealant, can be used to seal joints in those damaged gutters. Dab a little onto the cracks to keep your gutters leak-free—and keep rainwater flowing out and away from your home.

Painter’s caulk (or decorator’s caulk) is used, as its name suggests, just before decorating and painting. It’s the right choice for sealing crown molding, chair rails, and baseboards because it’s flexible and hides gaps between the wall and the finishes.

Whether you’re repairing a small hole or a sizable tear in your home’s vinyl siding, siding caulk can help. Simply choose a shade of exterior caulk that matches the hue of your exterior (even black caulk is available), and use a small dab to seal minor punctures, like nail holes. Cover larger holes or tears by applying caulk to the back of a scrap piece of siding, and covering the hole with the scrap piece.

Caulking between a countertop and a tile backsplash in the kitchen doesn’t just give your work space a “finished” look. It keeps crumbs, food items and worse yet, water, from getting behind your countertop and cabinets. Silicone caulk, which is moisture and mildew resistant, is the best caulk for the job. While you have your caulk gun out, make sure there’s a sturdy seal between your countertop and kitchen sink, too!

According to recent reports, when you don’t have any fluffy furniture pads on hand to stick on the undersides of flower pots and other decorative items, caulk can help. Turn your pots on their sides and apply a few dabs of silicone caulk to the bottoms of the pots. Allow the caulk to dry so the pots won’t stick to your floors. When they’re set, the silicone pads should keep the pot from scratching your hardwood.

In a recent development, one of the easiest ways to keep your asphalt or concrete driveway in good condition is to attend to cracks as soon as you notice them. The longer you wait, the better the chance that moisture will seep into the cracks, and make an even more fractured-looking mess of your driveway. Load your caulk gun with a quality, water-resistant asphalt crack sealant. Acrylic formulas are flexible and should fit into just about any nook or cranny.

Tech Report: It’s Not Too Late to Do the Lawn Maintenance You’ve Been Putting Off

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, many people assume lawn care ends when summer does, but autumn is when you’re laying the groundwork for next year’s success, says Allison Koenig, lawn and garden expert at Tractor Supply Company.
  • Earning perfect scores for ease of use, accuracy, and value in our hands-on test, this simple kit can help inform your fall lawn care routine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, many people assume lawn care ends when summer does, but autumn is when you’re laying the groundwork for next year’s success, says Allison Koenig, lawn and garden expert at Tractor Supply Company. “The work you do before winter, from mowing and fertilizing to leaf management and soil care, has a much bigger impact on spring performance than most homeowners realize,” she says. We spoke to Koenig and other lawn care experts to learn which fall lawn maintenance tasks you can still do even into early winter to improve the health and appearance of your lawn next spring, and what should be put off because it’s too late.

Earning perfect scores for ease of use, accuracy, and value in our hands-on test, this simple kit can help inform your fall lawn care routine.

The biggest misconception about fall lawn maintenance is that the lawn is dead because of cooler temperatures and doesn’t need attention anymore, claims Koenig. But this isn’t true; the lawn is just dormant, which is a significant difference. “A dormant lawn is still relying on the roots and reserves it built up in fall,” says Koenig. “Treat it like it’s done for the year and skip the prep work, and you’ll feel that mistake in spring.” Just be mindful that once the ground freezes or grass is fully dormant, it’s best to avoid aggressive projects like aerating, heavy raking, and major repairs. Winter is better spent protecting the lawn rather than trying to renovate it.

Industry observers note that pay a little attention to your lawn in fall and gain the rewards come the busy spring season. Experts suggest the following:.

Industry observers note that one of the simplest yet most important tasks in fall and winter is to keep your lawn free of debris, says Theresa Smith, senior vice president at NaturaLawn of America in Frederick, Maryland. “Fallen leaves and sticks can smother the grass, block sunlight, and trap moisture, leading to the grass becoming weak and susceptible to disease.” Regularly rake, mulch, and remove any large debris from the lawn to allow your grass to breathe and absorb as much sunlight as possible.

Mowing the lawn to the right height before winter arrives is an essential fall lawn task for preventing damage, says Smith. “Avoid cutting the grass too short, as this can lead to scalping and weakening the much-needed root system that it needs to survive winter,” she explains. “On the other hand, leaving the grass too long can also damage a lawn if it gets matted down with snow and ice, which can lead to disease and dying off.”.

Fall is one of the most effective times for weed control because many weeds are moving nutrients into their roots as they prepare for winter, which makes them more susceptible to treatment, says Brian Feldman, lead agronomist and senior director of technical operations at TruGreen. Consider the timing and the type of lawn, though. “For cool-season lawns, the ideal window is generally October through early November, while warm-season lawns can still benefit from treatment later in the fall, particularly for certain winter annual weeds,” says Feldman.

Before you put down any fertilizer or aerate, Wells Westmoreland, co-founder of Tomball Lawn Care Service in Tomball, Texas, recommends getting a soil test first. “The results tell you exactly which nutrients your lawn is missing (or has too much of), so when you go to buy fertilizer or hire someone to apply it for you, you’re getting the nutrients your yard actually needs,” he explains.

Fall can be a great time to aerate and overseed your lawn; however, the best time of year depends on the type of grass you have. “Cool-season grasses, such as Kentucky bluegrass or tall fescue, should be aerated and reseeded in late summer through fall, or mid-August to mid-October,” advises Smith. On the other hand, warm-season grasses, such as zoysias and Bermuda grasses, should be aerated when they are more actively growing, usually during late spring or early summer.

After a hot and dry summer, lawns begin to recover in the early fall, making it an ideal time to apply fertilizer in support of its growth, notes Smith. “Since daylight hours are shorter, the grass produces less top growth and directs the nutrients in the fertilizer toward root development, which helps keep the lawn healthy during colder months and helps yards that were fertilized to green-up quicker come springtime.” Some states have specific fertilizer restrictions in the late fall months, so be sure to check your state’s regulations before applying fertilizers.

Although winter typically reduces pest activity, some concerns can still arise. Mice, voles, and other small mammals may take refuge in your lawn during the colder months, causing damage by burrowing or feeding on grass roots, warns Smith. “Check for signs of pest damage and act, such as using traps or deterrents if necessary,” says Smith. “Similarly, look for any patches where the grass has turned brown and may be holding disease spores. Rake up the dead grass and bag it so it doesn’t spread before winter temperatures arrive.”.

Your grass doesn’t need nearly as much water this time of year, so decrease the frequency with which you water it. While you don’t need to stop, it’s a good time to pull back to avoid overwatering, which can cause large patches of your lawn to die off and invite fungus, disease, and root rot, says Westmoreland. “We see this a lot when sprinkler systems are still running on their summer schedule, so be sure to check your timer.”.

It’s critical to avoid sodding during colder months. “You’ll likely spend several hundred dollars or more hiring a contractor, and the new sod has a very low chance of taking root because it can’t establish itself in the cold,” warns Westmoreland. Instead, wait until spring and you’ll get a much better return on that investment.

Adding a lot of nitrogen right before the cold months encourages newly introduced growth to pop up. “The problem here is that new growth gets hit harder by the cold than more established turf, so nitrogen can end up killing off a substantial chunk of your lawn,” explains Westmoreland. “Save the nitrogen for when things warm back up; then, the new growth will be supported.”.

If you have a warm-season grass like St. Augustine, Bermuda, or zoysia, hold off on aeration and dethatching. These types of grasses only benefit from these processes when temperatures are much higher, as they’ll actively be growing during that time, indicates Westmoreland. “In the cold, the root zone on these grass types goes dormant, so aeration will just open up the turf to damage from the cold since the roots won’t be spreading as rapidly.” However, if you have cool-season grass like fescue or ryegrass, you can still move forward with these tasks.

Once soil temperatures have dropped and winter conditions have arrived, it is most likely too late to overseed cool-season lawns, notes Feldman.

For shoppers comparing DeWalt vs. Milwaukee, the battery platform and available tools are also worth considering.

Sources indicate that this pro-quality model was smaller and lighter than the other 18-volt drills we tested, making it easier to maneuver in confined workspaces. Its 575 inch-pounds of maximum torque handled hardened steel, concrete, and brick without binding and drove heavy-duty construction screws and lag bolts with ease.

In a recent development, even in concrete and brick, we found hammer mode unnecessary: Low speed and firm downward pressure were enough. However, when the bit reached about an inch deep, its straight shank began slipping in the chuck. Retightening allowed us to finish the hole, but slippage occurred three times during testing. What our tester states: “I really liked how the fresh Bosch hammer drill/driver felt—light, comfortable, and capable. In terms of comfort, as well as speed and torque, I preferred it over all of the other drills that I tested.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

In a recent development, the brushless motor delivers up to 486 inch-pounds of torque, while the ½-inch keyless metal chuck accepts larger-shank bits than the ⅜-inch chucks on some entry-level drills. Sources indicate that we like its compact body, soft-grip handle, and built-in LED—they make the drill a good option for working inside cabinets and other confined spaces. It has been revealed that we spent 27 hours testing 14 highly rated cordless drills, drilling more than 500 holes and installing 200 screws and bolts. We evaluated drilling speed and power in materials such as wood, steel, brick, and concrete, along with screwdriving control and the ability to seat larger fasteners. We also assessed chuck security, grip comfort, weight, maneuverability in confined spaces, and the usefulness of features such as work lights, speed controls, and adjustable clutches.

Industry observers note that features such as battery performance and included accessories also informed our value assessments. Each drill received scores from 0 (lowest) to 5 (highest) for build quality, ease of use, performance, and value. We then compared cumulative scores within each voltage range and selected the strongest performers for different users and project types.

Recent findings suggest that when choosing from different types of drills, start by matching their features to the needs of your projects. The most powerful cordless drill isn’t necessarily the best fit for occasional repairs, especially if its weight makes it tiring to use. As with all the best cordless tools, the ideal tool for the job tends to balance versatility, comfort, and value. Understanding how to use a drill also helps consumers get the most out of whatever drill you choose.

Sources indicate that battery voltage helps indicate a cordless drill’s capabilities, but it doesn’t measure power on its own. Motor design, gearing, and battery performance also matter. When choosing a battery-powered drill, consider the work you initiative to tackle rather than voltage alone.

Industry observers note that the distinction between 18V and 20V MAX can be confusing. These labels describe the same voltage class: 20V is the maximum initial battery voltage measured without a workload, while 18V is the nominal voltage. The difference isn’t a startup surge, nor does a 20V MAX label guarantee more power than an 18V model. Similarly, many drills marketed as 12V use batteries rated at 10.8V nominal.

Use these categories as a starting point:.

For masonry projects, knowing how to drill into concrete will help you select the appropriate tool, bit, and technique.

According to recent reports, battery capacity, measured in amp-hours (Ah), also matters. At the same voltage, a higher Ah rating generally means longer runtime, though actual results depend on the drill and workload. Smaller packs keep the tool lighter, while larger packs support longer work sessions but usually add weight and cost. A higher Ah rating alone doesn’t guarantee more drilling power. For occasional projects, a compact battery may be sufficient; for extended use, consider a larger pack or a spare.

Torque is the twisting force a drill delivers, while speed, measured in revolutions per minute (RPM), describes how rapidly the bit turns. A lower gear generally provides more torque for driving fasteners and drilling with larger bits. Higher speeds suit many smaller-bit drilling tasks, though the appropriate speed depends on the material and bit.

Most drills have an adjustable clutch that limits the torque transmitted to the chuck. When resistance reaches the selected setting, the clutch disengages to help prevent overdriving screws or stripping their heads. It responds to resistance rather than a preset screw depth, so choosing the right setting helps maintain control. Knowing how to change a drill bit also helps ensure the bit is properly seated and secured.

Look for at least 10 clutch settings to accommodate different fasteners and materials. A drilling machine with two gear settings offers more versatility, while a variable-speed trigger lets you fine-tune speed within the selected range.

A drill’s size and weight affect comfort, especially during extended use. Lightweight models can weigh about a pound, while heavy-duty cordless hammer drills may exceed 8 pounds. Extra power often adds weight, so choose a tool that balances capability with comfortable handling. Check whether the listed weight includes the battery, which can make a noticeable difference.

According to recent reports, A compact drill is easier to maneuver in confined spaces, and a smaller body doesn’t necessarily mean less power. Consider both weight and overall dimensions when comparing models.

Most cordless drills have keyless chucks for quick bit changes. Chuck capacity determines the largest bit-shank diameter the tool accepts, rather than the size of hole it can drill. Many general-purpose models have ⅜- or ½-inch chucks, while some compact drill/drivers use ¼-inch hex holders that accept only compatible hex-shank bits.

In a recent development, the best drill bits for a project must suit both the material and the drill’s chuck. Check compatibility before buying a bit set.

Recent findings suggest that corded drills sometimes come with a brushed motor. They are cheap and reliable, but the brushes eventually wear down and require replacement. Another challenge with brushed motors is that they create friction, which drains the battery faster in cordless models.

It has been revealed that the best cordless power drills often use a brushless motor. These virtually maintenance-free motors use the battery much more efficiently. However, brushless motors cost more. As a result, many budget cordless drills still use brushed motors.

For a typical DIYer, the difference is probably negligible. Those who want to maximize performance and runtime, particularly professional consumers, often choose a brushless cordless drill.

Sources indicate that like most modern battery-operated drills, the models in this guide use rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Runtime depends on battery capacity and workload, while charging time varies with the battery and charger. For extensive drilling, a kit with a spare battery lets you keep working while the depleted pack charges.

It has been revealed that note that manufacturer runtime claims often factor backup batteries into their runtime estimates. For instance, the specs on a drill that comes with two batteries, each lasting 1 hour, may list a 2-hour runtime.

Additionally, many cordless drills include a smart charger that replenishes the battery faster, usually within 15 to 60 minutes. A charge indicator allows you to monitor battery capacity.

Depending on your projects, these extras can improve comfort and convenience:.

Recent findings suggest that A refurbished cordless drill can help you save money or afford a higher-quality model while reducing waste. Unlike ordinary secondhand tools, refurbished models usually undergo inspection, repairs, and testing before resale. Standards vary by seller, however, so check what “refurbished,” “reconditioned,” or “renewed” means for the listing.

These tools may come from customer returns or have sustained shipping or warehouse damage. Don’t assume they were barely used or restored to like-new condition. You can browse refurbished drills at Amazon.

Industry observers note that walmart and other retailers also offer refurbished options. Keep these considerations in mind:.

According to recent reports, buy from a reputable source and inspect and test the drill promptly after delivery. If something is wrong, you’ll have time to request a return.

It has been revealed that our in-depth investigation of technologies and specifications above may have you feeling better equipped to choose the best power drill for your needs. That valuable information is underlined by examples of some of the top cordless drills currently available. Still, with so many options available, a few questions might remain. The following are answers to some of the most common questions.

It has been revealed that the primary use of a cordless drill is for drilling holes and driving screws. However, you can also get numerous attachments, which are sometimes included in cordless drill sets. Stirrers, for example, can mix paint and other liquids. You can also attach a sanding drum, a wire brush for rust removal, or a polishing bonnet. Our guide covers more uses for your cordless drill/driver.

Industry observers note that corded models were once more powerful tools. But today, equally powerful cordless models rival them. However, cordless models lose some of their power over the course of the charge, while corded models perform at a consistent level for as long as they’re plugged in.

Industry observers note that an electric screwdriver is usually much smaller, has less power, and cannot drill holes. The cordless drill can drill holes and also drive screws.

New and improved models enter the market all the time, so it’s difficult to name one brand as the best overall. Bosch, DeWalt, Makita, and Milwaukee all offer tools for different needs and budgets. Comparing individual models—including the best DeWalt drills—is more useful than choosing by brand alone.

Industry observers note that it very much depends on the amp hours of the battery and how hard the drill is working. A battery can last as little as 15 minutes, though many will run between 30 minutes and 1 hour. Buying a spare battery for your rechargeable drill lets you swap it out and keep working while the other charges.

In a recent development, brushless electric motors are more efficient and powerful than brushed motors. They often last longer, too. But higher performance also comes at a higher price. For occasional light-duty drilling, brushed cordless drills are more cost-effective.

According to recent reports, the best voltage depends on the user’s needs. For instance, 12-volt drills are inexpensive and perfectly capable of light-duty drilling and driving, while 18-volt drills deliver the higher torque and faster RPM needed for medium- and heavy-duty projects.

A right-angle drill solves problems when a standard drill can’t reach—navigating between studs, working inside cabinets, or tackling tight corners. While this makes these specialized power tools handy in these situations, who truly needs a right-angle drill?

The width of the head is perhaps the most crucial feature of a right-angle drill because it determines the space into which it can fit. However, there are several other key factors to take into account, including motor speed, power source, and weight. Ahead, learn more about these and other key attributes to think about when choosing the best right-angle drill.

It has been revealed that right-angle drills come in corded and cordless varieties, each with its own pros and cons. Cordless drills run on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery and offer the convenience and flexibility of not needing an electrical outlet or a cord. This lets you use them virtually anywhere.

According to recent reports, corded models, in comparison, require a standard electrical outlet. While these drills aren’t as convenient, a 120V power supply makes them more powerful while providing a reliable and constant power supply. Corded drills are also generally less expensive than cordless models. As with many power tools, spending more on a cordless model makes sense if it will see regular use. A less expensive corded model should suffice for DIYers who may use a right-angle drill only occasionally.

Industry observers note that size and weight determine a right-angle drill’s functionality and ease of use. Because a right-angle drill is meant to fit into tight spaces, size is crucial. Most right-angle drills have a head between 3 and 4 inches wide, so they can reach places standard corded and cordless power drills can’t.

Right-angle drills can also be short and lightweight enough to manage with one hand—although heavy-duty models typically come with a secondary handle.

It has been revealed that chuck size is also important. Most right-angle drills have a ⅜-inch chuck, which helps keep the head compact. Some larger models feature a ½-inch chuck for drilling larger holes or driving in bigger screws. These models typically have a wider head.

Right-angle drills have ergonomically shaped handles with rubberized grips that let you hold them securely with one hand while drilling. Many also have detachable side handles that let you apply more leverage with the other hand. Some manufacturers equip right-angle drills with paddle-style triggers that run the length of the handle. This feature lets you better regulate trigger pressure to control the drill’s speed.

Recent findings suggest that A drill’s speed determines how swiftly the tool can drill holes or drive screws. It also gives an indication of how much torque the drill produces if the manufacturer does not provide that information. Speed is measured in RPM and, in most cases, is directly related to the power source. Most cordless 18V right-angle drills top out at around 1,500 RPM, while some 20V drills can reach about 2,000 RPM.

In a recent development, corded right-angle drills have access to more power, which means they can produce more RPM. A corded 4-amp right-angle drill boasts around 2,400 RPM. While speed isn’t the same as torque, motors that can produce higher RPM are more powerful and thus capable of producing more torque.

Recent findings suggest that when assessing a cordless tool’s battery life, consider not only how long each charge lasts but also how long the battery itself will hold a charge before it needs replacing. Most batteries for right-angle cordless drills will last about 3 hours on a single charge with intermittent use and will take about 3 hours to recharge.

It has been revealed that lithium-ion batteries typically last about 3 years, or about 300 to 500 charging cycles, before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge. This doesn’t mean the battery will stop working altogether. As a battery nears the end of its life, it will simply last for a shorter period of time and require more frequent charging.

As with standard drills, right-angle drills are capable of using various types of bits and attachments. These drills are adept at drilling holes with standard drill bits or driving in screws with Phillips-head, flat, star, and other styles of screw-driving bits. These drills can also use socket attachments to drive bolts. Like other power tools, right-angle drills use a variety of accessories, including drill bits, screwdriver bits, chuck keys, and other accessories that can be misplaced. For this reason, many right-angle drills include a storage bag that holds the tool, accessories, batteries, and chargers all in one place for easy storage and transport.

Right-angle drills also often offer convenient features like LED lights that illuminate the work area and switches that make it easier to control the drill speed, permitting the user to increase or decrease the speed range to maximize control and improve torque.

For more information on how and where to best use a right-angle drill, read on for answers to some common questions about these power tools.

A right-angle drill has a geared head that rotates the chuck 90 degrees from the body’s axis, letting it reach tight spaces and drill or drive at angles a conventional drill can’t.

This versatile tool is helpful for a wide range of projects. It can be invaluable for fitting into tight spaces when working on a vehicle. A right-angle drill is also ideal for drilling between floor joists or wall studs, which are spaces that are typically too narrow for a standard drill.

A ⅜-inch drill has a chuck that can accommodate drill bits up to ⅜ inch. Similarly, a ½-inch drill has a larger chuck that can handle drill bits with a maximum diameter of ½ inch. A ½-inch drill generally offers more power and torque, making it suitable for drilling larger holes and tackling tougher materials. It’s commonly used in construction and heavy-duty applications.

A right-angle drill attachment is an accessory that can be added to a standard drill or driver to enable drilling and driving in tight or confined spaces that are difficult to access with a regular tool.

Industry observers note that yes. A right-angle drill can handle drilling tasks that require high torque and speed, depending on the type of drill. A model drill such as the Makita DA4031 or DeWalt DCD740 can drill large holes through floor joists, wall studs, and framing plates with ease.

According to recent reports, most cordless drills don’t require you to do a lot to maintain them, but there are few things you can do to keep them in tip-top shape. Wipe off any sawdust or debris after each use, paying close attention to the chuck and air vents. Remove the battery when the drill isn’t in use and store it in a cool place. Lubricate the chuck periodically by applying a small amount of machine oil to the chuck jaws to prevent stiffness.

The biggest danger with a right-angle drill is sudden kickback that can cause wrist injuries. If possible use two hands when operating a right-angle drill, one to control the trigger and the other on the back of the head to stabilize its motion. If that isn’t possible, brace the drill body or your arm against a solid object, like a wall stud, to prevent the tool from spinning out if it jams.
