As a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous. But in its diluted household form, the nitrogen-based super cleaner is a workhorse in the war on common household dirt and grime. Ammonia is readily available, inexpensive, and potent, so a little goes a long way.

Sources indicate that before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from. You may see “cloudy” or “sudsy” versions—that’s ammonia with soap added, which is generally used for such domestic cleaning chores as treating stained clothing or scrubbing stovetops. We recommend opting for “clear” ammonia, which is suited to a wider variety of tasks (and you can always add a tablespoon or two of dish soap to make clear ammonia sudsy). You’ll also find ammonia that’s scented with lemon or pine to temper its stinging odor.

According to recent reports, the harsh smell serves as a warning, though: Working with ammonia absolutely requires caution. Pure chemical ammonia can cause severe burns and respiratory challenges if it comes into contact with skin or is ingested. Even diluted in water, as is recommended for most cleaning purposes, ammonia can still be harmful.

According to recent reports, mixing ammonia and chlorine bleach creates a toxic gas called chloramine. Take great care not to combine them—doing so could have dire consequences.

It has been revealed that the most vital safety rule to remember is: Never mix ammonia with chlorine bleach. The result is a highly toxic chlorine gas that can produce headaches, seizures, and other symptoms. It’s crucial to keep this in mind if you’re using ammonia with laundry or to clean surfaces. You want to make absolutely sure not to mix it with a detergent or household cleaner that contains bleach.

Industry observers note that when using ammonia, be sure to wear chemical-resistant gloves and ventilate the area well. Be sure, too, to store it where pets and children can’t access it. Bearing these safety guidelines in mind, put ammonia to work around the home, as generations have done before us.

Industry observers note that to achieve streak-free mirrors, windows, and crystal, mix 1 tablespoon clear ammonia with 2 cups water in a spray bottle. Spritz the solution onto glass items and wipe immediately with a soft, lint-free cloth for windows and crystal; paper towels work fine for mirrors.

To remove stains on a concrete driveway, garage floor, or patio, mix 1 cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and apply it to the stain with a mop or large sponge. Let sit for about 20 minutes, and then scrub the stain with a bristled brush. Rinse the surface with clean water. If the stain isn’t completely gone after the area dries, repeat the process until you’re satisfied with the results.

If gold, silver, diamond, or platinum jewelry has lost its shine, mix 6 parts warm water to 1 part ammonia in a bowl (one that you don’t eat or cook with and add your jewelry. (Never use ammonia to clean pearls or other gems.) After 15 minutes, remove the jewelry with your gloved hand, and then gently scrape away any stubborn grime with a soft-bristled toothbrush (one that’s no longer in use or designated for cleaning). Allow it to soak for another 15 minutes, remove from the solution, and immediately rinse with warm water. Dispose of used ammonia solution down the drain while running the hot water. Polish the jewelry with a soft, lint-free cloth and let it dry.

Stubborn stains on cotton, polyester, or nylon fabrics are no match for a solution of ⅔ cup clear ammonia, ⅔ cup dish soap, 6 tablespoons of baking soda, and 2 cups warm water. Mix in a bowl or bucket and apply generously to stains with a sponge or spray bottle. Let the treatment sit for about 30 minutes, then launder as usual. For tougher stains like blood or grass, treat the stain again with a solution of 1 part ammonia and 1 part warm water.

Sources indicate that note: Do not use ammonia on wool or silk, which can eat through the delicate fabrics. And remember never to mix ammonia with any laundry products that contain bleach.

Tackle caked-on grease on stove burners with this trick. Place each burner in a separate sealable plastic bag filled with ¼ cup ammonia. Seal each bag to keep fumes at bay, and place in a sink or washtub for 8 to 12 hours. Open the bags in a ventilated area, and remove all grease and dirt easily with a quick scrub of dish soap and water. Once the gunk is gone, thoroughly rinse the burners with water to get rid of ammonia residue. Let dry completely before using.

Mix one part clear ammonia and one part hot water in a sprayer or other bottle. Apply generously to the stain by spritzing or with a sponge. After about 10 minutes of dwell time, place a clean old towel over the stain and press with an iron, blasting with steam, for about 20 seconds. Check your progress: The stain should start transferring to the towel. Repeat, with steam ironing and more ammonia solution if needed, until the stain is gone.

Ammonia is tough on every odor from fresh paint to burnt lasagna. Place a small container filled with about 1/2 cup of clear ammonia near an offending smell, being sure to keep the area ventilated, to absorb the nastiness within hours.

It has been revealed that heat the oven to 150 degrees, and set a large pot of water on the stove to boil. Turn off the oven and open the windows to ventilate the kitchen. Place a sturdy container, such as a glass measuring cup or metal bowl, filled with ½ cup ammonia on the oven’s top shelf. Place the pot of boiled water on the bottom shelf. Close the oven and let sit for 8 to 12 hours, then remove the containers of ammonia and water. Open the oven door and air air out for at least an hour before cleaning. Because the grime has basked in ammonia fumes, it should be loosened and easy to remove with a sponge, warm water, and dish soap.

This method is only recommended for electric ovens, because mixing ammonia with gas can be dangerous. If you choose to use this method on your gas oven, make sure that the pilot light and gas lines are turned off.

To clean and disinfect kitchen and bath tiles, mix ¼ cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and use a sponge or mop to liberally apply the solution to the tile. Use a soft-bristled brush to scrub any particularly stubborn areas. Finish up by rinsing the surface with clean water and your sponge or mop.

According to recent reports, ammonia’s strong scent can deter unwanted critters. Fill a saucer with clear, unscented ammonia, or saturate a rag or cotton balls with it. Then place in areas that attract pests, such as near garbage cans where raccoons prowl or beside cracks in the basement where mice enter. The smell will remind the varmints of predators, so they’re likely to catch a whiff and turn away, unharmed. That noted, make sure to keep the ammonia deterrent out of reach of kids and pets.

Tesla intends to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The organization’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the manufacturer is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images.

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

According to recent reports, tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Recent findings suggest that current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

Industry observers note that for anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

Tesla hasn’t mentioned which customers will receive their trucks or how it prepares to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The firm intends to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

According to recent reports, musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the firm can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

This short latest article of mine has now been published in the Notre Dame Law Review. The Introduction:.

Recent findings suggest that there are many important big-picture questions about original meaning and the Free Speech, Free Press, Assembly, and Petition Clauses. This short Essay will leave those questions for others. Instead, it will offer as illustrations some specific, concrete questions—and, in some instances, answers—about original meaning and the freedom of expression. I hope these narrow illustrations can help us think about the broader questions.

From the table of contents, which should illustrate the subjects I cover:.

I. Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals" B. Symbolic Expression C. Civil Liability II. Scant Evidence: Provoking a Riot III. Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels.

Whether courts should shift the constitutional law of free expression to a more originalist footing is an key and difficult question. Perhaps it's a question that should be resolved entirely as a matter of constitutional theory—maybe such an approach is required by proper interpretive principles, or maybe it's forbidden by other principles (for instance, having to do with precedent).

But it's also possible that the answer may rest in part on how practically usable an originalist framework is likely to be. And to consider that, it's helpful to have in mind some practical questions. Some are already familiar, for instance questions related to damages liability in libel cases, obscenity law, and the like. This short Essay has aimed to help supplement those familiar examples with some others that haven't been much discussed; I hope others who think about the topic can find them useful.

I expect I'll post excerpts from the article in the coming days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the Newly introduced World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

Sources indicate that how many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

Recent findings suggest that if you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Sources indicate that definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” notes Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”.

Sources indicate that it’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”.

Sources indicate that one option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”.

For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” indicates Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”.

In a recent development, this is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

Sources indicate that before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

It has been revealed that composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

It has been revealed that don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they quickly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”.

It has been revealed that it’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Sources indicate that generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

Sources indicate that A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

It has been revealed that understanding the two types of wood stoves, the materials used to make them, and their heating capacity are all vital when shopping for one of these appliances. Ahead, learn more about these and other important attributes of the best wood stoves.

According to recent reports, wood stoves are available in two types: catalytic and noncatalytic. Catalytic wood stoves differ from noncatalytic in that they produce fewer exhaust fumes and burn more efficiently. In addition to burning wood, catalytic wood stoves also have a combustor that burns smoke and byproducts. This design allows the stove to burn cleaner with a slower burn rate, conserving fuel. Efficiency ratings for a catalytic wood stove range between 63 and 84 percent, making them ideal options for use as a primary source of heat.

Industry observers note that noncatalytic stoves are cheaper but not as efficient. They are better suited for use as a supplemental heater.

Most wood stoves are made from one of three materials: cast iron, plate steel, or soapstone. Cast iron, the most commonly used material, heats up swiftly and retains warmth longer than other materials. However, it does crack more easily and is more expensive than other materials.

Plate steel, also a common material used in wood stoves, is durable and retains heat well, though not as well as cast iron. Soapstone is a high-end material for wood stoves. It retains heat better than cast iron, burns cleaner than other materials, and can burn for 24 hours or longer on a single load. Most wood stoves consist of either soapstone or plate steel with a cast-iron door.

Sources indicate that A wood stove’s heating capacity determines how large of a space the wood stove can keep warm when it’s running with a full load of wood. The heating area for most stoves ranges from around 1,200 square feet for a small stove to as much as 2,200 square feet (or more) for a large model.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that, unlike a home’s central heating, which distributes heat through ductwork, a wood stove emanates heat from the fire, so the heat isn’t evenly distributed. The farther someone is from the wood stove, the cooler the temperature will be.

Recent findings suggest that the heat output of a wood stove is measured in BTUs (British thermal units). Wood stoves range in BTU output from around 50,000 to 80,000 BTUs. The more BTUs, the greater the size of the space the wood stove can heat. A large 70,000-BTU wood stove can warm up to 2,200 square feet. While BTU level is a great indication of how powerful the stove is, not all manufacturers provide BTU information for their stoves.

A wood stove’s burn time is the amount of time one load of wood lasts before the stove requires reloading. Each stove’s burn time is determined by how much wood it can hold as well as the heat output of the stove, which can be regulated using the stove’s damper. The firewood type being used also affects burn time. Hardwoods burn more efficiently than softwood, which is less dense and therefore burns more quickly and at lower temperatures.

In a recent development, wood-burning stoves produce toxic emissions; they create carbon monoxide, which can be deadly if not properly vented outside. Wood stoves are regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency, which performs safety tests on wood stoves to make sure they’re safe for consumer use. The emission limit for wood stoves is 2 grams to 2.5 grams per hour, depending on the type of wood. Catalytic stoves produce well under the EPA’s maximum, with emissions of around 0.5 grams per hour. Never buy a wood stove that is not certified by the EPA.

According to recent reports, perhaps the most important thing to consider when shopping for a wood stove is where it will go in the living space. Most freestanding wood stoves take up a significant chunk of real estate since they measure about 3 feet wide and 2 feet deep and require a buffer around them for safety. Portable models are much smaller—about 20 inches high and 10 inches deep and less than 40 pounds—allowing them to fit in the trunk of a car for a camping trip.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that the size of the stove also affects the size of wood they can burn. A standard freestanding or insert wood stove can hold logs up to 18 inches long, whereas portable models can typically handle logs that measure about 8 inches long.

In addition to providing a source of heat, wood stoves also create an ambience that’s similar to a wood-burning fireplace. Most wood stoves have glass windows that allow people sitting around the stove to watch the burning logs.

Some wood stoves also serve as a cooking stove, with flat tops that will support a frying pan or pot. Stoves with cooking functions are typically designed for outdoor use and camping trips.

Sources indicate that the best place for a wood stove is as close to the center of the area requiring heat as possible. This allows the stove to radiate warmth in all directions, better heating the space.

Hardwoods—which include oak, maple, ash, and birch—are the best-burning woods. They will burn longer and hotter than softwoods like pine and also contain the least amount of pitch and sap inside of them.

According to recent reports, use a brush to sweep up any debris or ash that was not collected by the fireplace’s ash pan. Next, use a wire brush to clean off any buildup inside the flue pipe. Wipe off the exterior of the wood stove with a dry cloth. Be sure to avoid using liquids, which can leave streaks.

The average wood stove should last between 10 and 20 years, depending on usage and care.

In a recent development, it is safe to leave a wood fireplace on overnight, as long as you follow a few precautions. Allow the wood to burn for a few hours before going to bed. Before turning in for the night, add ash to the burning logs to dampen the flames and slow the burning process. Next, close the stove air vents to reduce the size of the fire, ensuring it will be safe even when burning through the night.

In a recent development, yes. Latest Update: Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.
  • In a recent development, what makes a yard an eyesore?
  • Sources indicate that the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

In a recent development, what makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

Sources indicate that the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

According to recent reports, unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can swiftly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

In a recent development, vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can promptly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception concern if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes indicates.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can rapidly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty claims. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

Recent findings suggest that fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be newly introduced to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker notes. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker says. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

Industry observers note that while low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes claims. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

Sources indicate that “There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty notes. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Recent findings suggest that broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

Sources indicate that while they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland notes. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland states. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our upcoming neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Recent findings suggest that kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty states. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

A simple strand of string lights can transform a plain backyard into an inviting outdoor space. Compared with many other types of exterior house lights, string lights are among the most affordable and easiest to install. If you want to hang string lights outdoors, consider light type, size and shape, brightness, and color. A weather-resistant design, a lengthy cord, and a remote or app control can make the lights safer and easier to use.

According to recent reports, most outdoor string lights feature LED, incandescent, solar, or battery-operated bulbs. Each type varies in durability, energy efficiency, and lifespan. When shopping for outdoor string lights, consider which type of lighting is most suitable for the space.

Sources indicate that since outdoor string lights are exposed to the elements, it’s vital to select a set that can withstand rainy conditions and heavy gusts of wind. It’s inconvenient to take the string lights down every time inclement weather is forecast.

Sources indicate that first, check the product description to determine if the lights are intended for outdoor use. Using indoor lighting outside creates a potential fire hazard. Second, make sure the product is water-resistant (or waterproof, as even spots under a porch or gazebo roof can grow damp in bad weather). Weather-resistant lights can handle direct exposure to water and feature watertight seals to protect their interior components from accumulating moisture and causing safety challenges.

String light bulbs are available in a variety of styles and shapes, which can give the strands a unique aesthetic.

According to Friedman, “You’ll also want to look for shatterproof bulbs, ideally LED, since they’re cooler and more efficient.”.

When choosing a bulb size, consider the available outdoor space, ease of installation, and desired look.

According to recent reports, small bulbs are a good pick for small outdoor spaces or garden lighting; they won’t overpower a space or other outdoor decorations. These bulbs are generally more subtle, providing gentle background lighting. They provide less light and are commonly chosen for decorative purposes.

According to recent reports, large bulbs are more striking and offer a bolder look. Their larger size can provide more direct illumination. Generally brighter, they’re well suited to larger spaces that need more lighting. Large decorative bulbs, such as globe bulbs and Edison bulbs, can make a style statement.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that bulb size can affect installation. String lights with small bulbs are generally lightweight and easier to maneuver. They may be easier to install than string lights with larger, heavier, and bulkier bulbs.

Most globe outdoor string light bulbs come in one of three bulb sizes:.

Most Edison-style string light bulbs are an S14 bulb size, which is a medium-size, oval-shaped bulb that’s 32 millimeters (just over 1.25 inches) in diameter.

When it comes to the appearance of outdoor string lights, brightness and color temperature are two of the most important factors to consider.

Lumens measure the amount of light output from a bulb—the more lumens, the brighter the bulb. When deciding on bulb brightness, take into account the desired lighting effect. String light bulbs can range from 5 to more than 100 lumens per bulb. Users often choose string lights for their glowy appearance rather than their brightness, so lower lumens often do just fine to set the mood. Lumens are different from wattage, as wattage measures how much power a bulb consumes and not necessarily how bright a light appears.

In a recent development, lighting color temperature is measured using the Kelvin temperature scale. This scale measures how warm or cool the light appears. Lower numbers on the Kelvin scale look warmer, and higher numbers look cooler.

In a recent development, most home lighting falls between 2000K and 6000K. Bulbs around 2700K have a cozy, warm white color with a yellow hue, while bulbs over 5000K offer stark, crisp lighting with a blue hue. Warm lighting makes a space look more cozy and inviting, while cool lighting can often appear harsh, especially at night. For this reason, warmer bulbs are generally preferred for ambient outdoor lighting.

Sources indicate that outdoor string lights typically come in lengths of 10, 25, 35, 50, and 100 feet. When choosing the ideal wire length, consider the size of the outdoor space and the lighting layout.

Patio string lights can outline garden borders, wrap around banisters and trees, or suspend over seating spaces. The best way to determine the necessary wire length is to use a piece of twine to measure where the lights will go. If the lights require corded power, make sure to include enough length to reach the outlet, or keep an extension cord handy.

Industry observers note that to line one side of an average balcony or small porch, a 10-foot string of outdoor patio lights may do the trick. A small 8-foot-long by 6-foot-wide patio space typically requires 25 to 50 feet of string lighting. A medium 12-foot-square outdoor space may need 50 to 100 feet of string lighting, depending on the desired layout. For more spacious areas or to illuminate a large event, more than 100 feet of string lighting is usually necessary.

It has been revealed that in terms of wire strength, Friedman recommends commercial-grade stringers with heavy-gauge wire. “This will hold tension much better, and the extra insulation will provide safety and durability.” He adds that “these stringers are much heavier than your average consumer string lights, so make sure you mount them securely.”.

For those who want to upgrade from basic string lights, consider a product with extra features like color-changing bulbs, dimming options, and remote control or app operation. As we discovered in our tests, consumers are able to create entirely different moods by selecting different bulb colors.

Recent findings suggest that string lights can instantly transform a typical yard or patio into a warm and inviting space, but choosing the right set of lights is a must for creating the desired atmosphere. White light is the most effective lighting color since it is closest to natural light. Warm white lights have a cozy, inviting yellow tinge, making them a popular pick for outdoor lighting. Colorful bulbs are often chosen for the ambience they create rather than their lighting ability. These lights add a decorative flair and can be a fun addition for different seasons and holidays.

Recent findings suggest that the Lemontec Commercial-Grade Outdoor String Lights offer fifteen 11-watt incandescent bulbs and are one of the best options in the lineup for those seeking a brighter set of outdoor string lights. Plus, additional sets can be connected for even more illumination.

According to recent reports, yes, some weather-resistant and weatherproof string lights can be left outdoors. Be sure to check their specifications to ensure the lights can handle changing weather and temperature conditions year-round.

According to recent reports, the easiest way to hang lights is to use existing fixtures or to wrap them around columns and railings surrounding a patio. If necessary, create hanging options by installing metal hooks, heavy-duty sticky hooks, or nails where needed.

No, outdoor string lights typically use very little electricity—especially LED models, which are more energy efficient than incandescent.

Breaking: Can You Really Turn Your Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

It has been revealed that snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can rapidly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

It has been revealed that the short answer is “yes, maybe,” stated David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”.

Accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Industry observers note that officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:.

Recent findings suggest that modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

Officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Sources indicate that regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):.

It has been revealed that in "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again.".

Although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.

In a recent development, it is not for me at my time of life to learn a new language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

It has been revealed that according to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Sources indicate that four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

But lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times.

He labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:.

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

Though in wintertime a window seat affords postcard-perfect views of snow-covered tree branches, it’s not necessarily the most comfortable perch on a cold day. During the chilly season, so much heat can escape through the panes of glass as well as through any cracks or gaps around the window frame that you’ll want to wrap up in a blanket, or at least put on a sweater, before you risk sitting so close to a window. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average home loses as much as a third of its energy as a result of poor window insulation. Luckily, there are several ways to mitigate this loss. Follow these best practices for how to insulate windows, and you can secure a warmer winter with just one weekend of work.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Decades of exposure to the elements can wear away one of your main defenses against heat loss: exterior caulking. Once this begins to crumble, cracks can start to form around the window frame. If your windows are drafty, take swift action to replace the exterior caulking along the window frames before the weather takes a turn for the worse.

Recent findings suggest that check the weather before you begin the process. For successful application of caulking, you’ll want clear skies for 24 hours—no snow or rain—and, ideally, temperatures above 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

It has been revealed that use a putty knife to scrape window edges clean out the old caulking and peeling paint. Then, wipe the surface clean of any remnants with a damp rag. Let the surface dry for a few hours so the fresh caulking will readily adhere. It’s best to start the project early in the day to allow enough dry time. You could also leave it to dry overnight.

Load your no-drip caulking gun with a cartridge of silicone exterior caulk and hold it at a 45-degree angle in order to get deep into the cracks around the window frame. Apply a solid, continuous bead of caulking between the frame and the siding, all the way around the window. Any caulk that oozes out of the crack should be pushed in gently with a putty knife.

Allow this to cure overnight to provide the best protection from wind and moisture.

Industry observers note that the sash, the part of the window that moves to open and close, is the area most homeowners zero in on when they’re trying to improve window insulation. While this area is important, don’t neglect the glass itself or ignore other draft-curbing solutions. Take a multistep approach to insulating the inside of your windows by employing weatherstripping, window film, and energy-smart window treatments. Though we present this step-by-step approach as a process, you’ll still gain energy savings if you don’t complete every step.

Industry observers note that note: When you’re selecting replacement weatherstripping, closely consider the pros and cons of each material. As with many building materials, you get what you pay for in terms of lifespan. Felt, for example, is a common pick for its low price, but it can fail within only a few years. Adhesive-backed foam and tubular gasket stripping, on the other hand, are both cost-effective compression seals that work reliably and provide 3 to 5 years of protection from the cold.

In a recent development, if your weatherstripping is worn or crumbling, it’s time to remove and replace it. Adhesive-backed stripping can simply be pulled up by hand. If the weatherstripping is attached with nails or screws, however, you must first remove the fasteners with a claw hammer or drill before you can lift it away. Once you’ve pulled the weatherstripping off, wipe down the window sash with a damp rag or paper towels and household cleaner. Allow it to dry thoroughly.

Measure your sash carefully, then cut the weatherstripping of your choice to length. Start as close as you can to the end of one side of the sash, peel off any adhesive backing, then carefully press the weatherstripping into place on the sash, making your way carefully to the other end.

“One insulating technique I love and have done many times requires the trim to be off (if, say, you’re installing a new window or entry door): fill the voids between the door or window jamb and the rough framing with low-expanding foam insulation.”.

—Mark Clement, Contributing Writer.

Sources indicate that with the new weatherstripping in place, you’ll want to double up your efforts with a window insulation kit. In addition to retaining up to 55 percent of your home’s heat in winter, this type of window covering will reflect heat and block UV rays from passing through uncovered windows, lowering indoor temperatures in summer and saving energy costs year-round. Before you proceed, check to see if your windows are still under warranty; the addition of window film may void the contract. If you’re in the clear, select the best quality insulating window film you can find for the job. Cheap versions can make the outdoors seem darker and even somewhat blurry. While that’s not a massive issue for windows in some rooms, for more prominent windows, you may want to invest in higher-quality film that causes little to no loss of clarity and light.

Note: Cheaper methods that produce a similar insulating effect involve heat-and-shrink film or even bubble wrap, but these are often less attractive options that hamper or prevent the use of the windows, or hinder visibility. These inexpensive fixes, however, can be effective, easy to apply, and energy-efficient solutions for basement or attic windows.

According to recent reports, whichever method you choose, installation instructions vary from product to product. In general, start by washing the windowpanes so that no dust or lint gets trapped during application, then follow the manufacturer’s directions for installing the window film.

It has been revealed that best Home blackout curtains keep out up to 99% of light with triple-weave polyester construction and a layer of black yarn. Read the review.

Sources indicate that for one last defense against heat loss and drafts, consider hanging thermal curtains. For best insulating effects, install the curtain rod above and past each window on either side so the curtains fully cover the window frame. If it’s not appropriately installed, make adjustments to the rod’s position to maximize heat retention. While other window treatments like blinds or sheers offer some protection from drafts, a set of heavy curtains that you draw shut after dusk can cut heat loss by up to 17 percent.

Whether you ultimately decide to complete just one or all of these steps, you’ll still reap benefits. The more solutions you employ, however, the greater heat retention and energy savings you’ll see, and potentially not just in winter, but all year-round. If you’ve tried all these methods and still have poor window insulation, it might be time to replace your home’s windows.

Instead of just guessing, plumbers, drain-cleaning technicians and experienced property owners can visually inspect accessible portions of a line for signs of root intrusion, buildup, standing water, cracks, offsets and other visible problems before deciding what comes next.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is designed for those longer, more demanding inspections. A rigid push cable, self-leveling camera and bright adjustable lighting help operators work farther into sewer lines while recording what they find along the way.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is a professional-grade pipe inspection system built to provide a clear view inside longer drain and sewer lines.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera houses its inspection equipment in a wheeled system that moves effortlessly between jobs while keeping cables easy to manage.

Industry News: Before or After the Snow? Here’s the Right Time to Salt Your Driveway This Winter

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.
  • The Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months.
  • Salting before a significant storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

The Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

Sources indicate that it depends. Salting before a significant storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

Strategy to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

According to recent reports, it’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

The best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, says.

Apply salt before and after a substantial storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

It has been revealed that “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, says. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

In a recent development, if only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

It has been revealed that “The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how big the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski says. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland indicates. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

It has been revealed that rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski indicates. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

Yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski claims.

There’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

But weighing a little over 40 pounds, it’s not a countertop appliance you want to move around—and it’s not cheap either. Which begs the question: Is the Nugget Ice Maker Pro worth the space and investment? I tested it to find out.

The Nugget Ice Maker Pro started producing ice within minutes of setup, and filling the entire 3.5-pound bucket took less than 90 minutes. If you emptied it after each fill, that would mean you could make up to 60 pounds of ice in about 24 hours. We used it for everything from filling our massive water bottles and making super-cold fruit smoothies to hosting a house full of teenagers on Halloween.

But that impressive quantity isn’t this machine’s best feature—the ice it makes is. Popularized by drive-thru restaurants like Sonic, nugget ice has a somewhat soft, air-pocketed texture that soaks up your drink’s flavor while also being easy to chew. That crunchable quality makes it as perfect for iced coffee, lemonade, and specialty cocktails as it is for blending smooth in a shake.

Recent findings suggest that when we first set up the GoveeLife, we put it in our kitchen, since that seemed logical. Luckily, moving it to the garage was incredibly easy, and because the 4.9-liter water reservoir is detachable, we just carry that part inside when it’s time to refill.

It has been revealed that scooping from the Ice Maker Pro is equally straightforward. In terms of maintenance, the 10-minute quick-cleaning mode handles most of the work, but you’ll also want to run the 30-minute deep descaling mode and hand-wash the removable parts occasionally.

Industry observers note that at roughly 43 pounds and almost $500, the GoveeLife Ice Maker isn’t small, and it isn’t cheap. But if you have the space and love nugget ice, its sleek finish, customizable RGB lighting, and quality cubes will be right at home in your kitchen or home bar. Regardless of location, however, the appeal is the same: quick production, consistent nuggets, and enough capacity to handle everyday drinks and entertainment. We love ours, and it’s officially staying put.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Torres v. Carlson, currently pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada.".

Recent findings suggest that assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

It has been revealed that nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking matter with the district court's decisions to:.

(1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;.

(2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,.

(3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

How to Shovel the Trickiest Surfaces the Right Way, From Pavers to Your Roof

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.
  • Sources indicate that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces.
  • According to recent reports, “Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Sources indicate that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s key to solidify your shoveling plan before the first snow flies.

According to recent reports, “Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

Sources indicate that shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” states grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” claims Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

In a recent development, A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” states Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” notes Flores.

The fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, notes Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, indicates Lopez.

It has been revealed that just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

Industry observers note that “Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” indicates Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

Industry observers note that A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

Industry observers note that “Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” notes Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

It has been revealed that after a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

Sources indicate that pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” states Lopez. “.

Try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

According to recent reports, “Before winter arrives, plan where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” says Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

It has been revealed that also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

Sources indicate that safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” indicates Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural concern.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

To stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” indicates Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” says Schwab.

In a recent development, sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

According to recent reports, “Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” states Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

Obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” says Flores.

It has been revealed that when choosing an electric heater for basements, there are a few variables to consider, beginning with the basic type, power source, and heating capacity. Once you know the kind and size you’ll need, look for other features to improve the overall experience.

Choose the type that best fits the way you will use the space. Four heating technologies predominate: oil-filled radiators, fan-forced, infrared, and micathermic.

While non-electric space heaters are available, electricity is by far the most popular choice. Electricity is clean and simple with no unpleasant fumes, and, generally speaking, it is very safe.

Heating capacity is specified in watts (W). Space heaters may have multiple settings to save energy. As a rough guide, experts recommend 10W per square foot. So, if a basement is 100 square feet, it would need a 1,000W heater.

Physical size and appearance tend to be more important in a basement that’s used regularly. The smaller the size, the less the unit will impact the decor of the space, yet some units are more visually appealing than others. They vary from plain and functional to sleek and modern, to those that mimic the look of a real fireplace or stove.

Portability will be vital if the heater is moved around to different parts of the basement, rather than one that is permanently situated. Lightweight models needn’t be just for the basement but can be used around the house to provide heat where needed.

While electric space heaters are inherently safer than those that produce a live flame, most incorporate additional space heater safety features. Overheating sensors are common, turning the device off if vents get blocked or the temperature rises beyond a preset level. Tip-over sensors automatically shut the heater off should it get knocked down. Some models have cool-touch exteriors, and a few have child locks to prevent accidental operation.

Recent findings suggest that most space heaters include other user-friendly features like thermostats, timers, and Wi-Fi connectivity. Remote control is one of the most popular features, especially for larger rooms.

Sources indicate that any source of heat, whether electric or propane, has the potential to cause a fire. While many space heaters have built-in safety features like tip-over sensors, there are a few simple steps you can take to make sure your home is safe.

It has been revealed that electrical tape comes in plenty of colors, but each has a purpose. Here's what the common shades mean in U.S. electrical work.

According to recent reports, being a DIY electrician is one way homeowners like to save a little money over expensive repairs. However, there are safety concerns when it comes to doing your own electrical work. Electrical tape color meanings help electricians identify wires and make sense of connections that might otherwise look identical. The trouble is that colors don’t always mean the same thing.

Learn what the common colors usually mean, how electricians use them, and why a strip of tape can’t confirm a wire’s purpose.

Recent findings suggest that electricians use colored tape to identify wires, especially when several look alike. In the United States, the colors commonly mean:.

Industry observers note that these colors aren’t universal. The National Electrical Code sets rules for identifying neutral and grounding wires, but most hot-wire colors follow common practices rather than strict requirements. For example, orange can have a specific meaning in certain commercial electrical systems. Its purpose depends on the wiring, so electricians can’t rely on color alone.

Electricians often wrap colored tape around the ends of wires to tell them apart. Manufacturers such as 3M make tape specifically for identifying different electrical connections.

According to recent reports, tape can also show when a wire serves a different purpose than its original color suggests. For example, electricians may mark a white wire with black tape to identify it as a hot wire in certain situations. Electrical codes limit when and how they can make these changes.

Recent findings suggest that however, tape color alone can’t confirm a wire’s purpose or whether it carries electricity. Previous repairs, incorrect markings, or different labeling practices can cause confusion. Before starting electrical work, a qualified person should identify the circuit and test that the power is off. Homeowners who encounter unfamiliar or conflicting wire markings should have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring.

On August 10, 2026, Defendant Darius Drew entered a guilty plea to one count of Aggravated Assault and one count of Carrying a Pistol Without a License. Mr. Drew appeared before the Court for a sentencing hearing on November 13, 2026. At the hearing, the Court sentenced Mr. Drew to an aggregate term of incarceration of 24 months followed by 3 years of supervised release, with the execution of all but the 6 months he already served suspended in favor of 18 months of supervised probation.

In a recent development, in addition to the standard conditions of probation, the Court required that Mr. Drew participate in a comprehensive mental health assessment and treatment as deemed necessary by the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency ("CSOSA"), undergo a substance abuse assessment and complete all treatment deemed necessary by CSOSA, and complete 90 hours of community service. He is required to register as a gun offender in the District of Columbia and remain registered for two years following the expiration of his period of probation. The Court entered an order requiring Mr. Drew to stay away from the location of the offense. During the period of probation, Mr. Drew is required to participate in either a GED program or vocational training and to maintain or seek employment. The Court also required Mr. Drew to appear before the Court for regularly-scheduled probation review hearings.

Sources indicate that because Mr. Drew was 19 years old at the time of this offense, he requested through counsel that he be sentenced under the Youth Rehabilitation Act ("YRA"), D.C.
